#10181. QIMMA قِمّة ⛰: A Quality-First Arabic LLM Leaderboard

QIMMA validates benchmarks before evaluating models, ensuring reported scores reflect genuine Arabic language capability in LLMs.

If you've been tracking Arabic LLM evaluation, you've probably noticed a growing tension: the number of benchmarks and leaderboards is expanding rapidly, but are we actually measuring what we think we're measuring?

We built QIMMA قمّة (Arabic for "summit"), to answer that question systematically. Instead of aggregating existing Arabic benchmarks as-is and running models on them, we applied a rigorous quality validation pipeline before any evaluation took place. What we found was sobering: even widely-used, well-regarded Arabic benchmarks contain systematic quality issues that can quietly corrupt evaluation results.

This post walks through what QIMMA is, how we built it, what problems we found, and what the model rankings look like once you clean things up.

Arabic is spoken by over 400 million people across diverse dialects and cultural contexts, yet the Arabic NLP evaluation landscape remains fragmented. A few key pain points have motivated this work:

Translation issues. Many Arabic benchmarks are translations from English. This introduces distributional shifts. Questions that feel natural in English become awkward or culturally misaligned in Arabic, making benchmark data less representative of how Arabic is naturally used.

Absent quality validation. Even native Arabic benchmarks are often released without rigorous quality checks. Annotation inconsistencies, incorrect gold answers, encoding errors, and cultural bias in ground-truth labels have all been documented in established resources.

Reproducibility gaps. Evaluation scripts and per-sample outputs are rarely released publicly, making it hard to audit results or build on prior work.

Coverage fragmentation. Existing leaderboards cover isolated tasks and narrow domains, making holistic model assessment difficult.

To illustrate where QIMMA sits relative to existing platforms:

QIMMA is the only platform combining all five properties: open source, predominantly native Arabic content, systematic quality validation, code evaluation, and public per-sample inference outputs.

QIMMA consolidates 109 subsets from 14 source benchmarks into a unified evaluation suite of over 52,000 samples, spanning 7 domains:

A few things stand out about this design:

This is the methodological heart of QIMMA. Before running a single model, we applied a multi-stage validation pipeline to every sample in every benchmark.

Each sample was independently evaluated by two state-of-the-art LLMs:

We chose two models with strong Arabic capability but different training data compositions, so that their combined judgment is more robust than either alone.

Each model scores a sample against a 10-point rubric, with binary scores (0 or 1) per criterion:

A sample is eliminated if either model scores it below 7/10. Samples where both models agree on elimination are dropped immediately. However, where only one model flags a sample, it proceeds to human review in Stage 2.

Flagged samples are reviewed by native Arabic speakers with cultural and dialectal familiarity. Human annotators make final calls on:

For culturally sensitive content, multiple perspectives are considered, since "correctness" can genuinely vary across Arab regions.

The pipeline revealed recurring quality issues across benchmarks; not isolated errors, but systematic patterns reflecting gaps in how benchmarks were originally constructed.

False or mismatched gold indices, factually wrong answers, missing or raw text answers.

Corrupt or illegible text, spelling and grammar errors, and duplicate samples.

Stereotype reinforcement and monolithic generalizations about diverse communities.

Misalignment of gold answers with evaluation protocols.

Code benchmarks required a different intervention. Rather than discarding samples, we refined the Arabic problem statements in 3LM's Arabic adaptations of HumanEval+ and MBPP+, leaving task identifiers, reference solutions, and test suites completely unchanged.

QIMMA uses LightEval, EvalPlus and FannOrFlop as its evaluation framework, chosen for consistency, multilingual community adoption, and reproducibility.

QIMMA standardizes prompting by question format, with six template types:

All prompts are in Arabic. For MizanQA and ArabCulture, benchmark-specific system prompts from the original papers are preserved.

Results as of April 2026; covering top 10 evaluated models. Visit the live leaderboard for current rankings.

#10178. Your AI Pipeline Works. But Can You Trust It?

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI is becoming a part of almost everything we do in technology today. Whether it's detecting fraudulent transactions, assessing credit risk, forecasting demand, or personalizing customer experiences, organizations are increasingly relying on AI to make faster and smarter decisions.

And naturally, when we talk about building AI systems, most of the conversation revolves around model accuracy, performance, and deployment. We spend considerable time making sure our models are trained well, our pipelines run efficiently, and our systems can handle production workloads.

But here's something we don't always pay enough attention to: Can we actually trust the data feeding these models?

After all, even the most sophisticated AI model can produce misleading results if the underlying data is incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrectly interpreted. What's interesting is that these problems don't always show up as technical failures. Sometimes, everything appears to be working perfectly fine.

Imagine a financial institution that has recently deployed an AI-powered loan risk assessment system. The team has spent months preparing the data, training the model, testing its performance, and finally moving it into production.

The deployment goes smoothly. Data pipelines are running on schedule, predictions are being generated, and all the monitoring dashboards are green.

A few weeks later, however, the business team notices something unusual. The model has started classifying more customers as high risk than expected.

The data science team checks the model configuration. Nothing has changed. The engineering team reviews the pipelines. All jobs have completed successfully. Even the infrastructure looks healthy.

It turns out that an upstream source system changed the definition of a customer income field from annual gross income to annual net income. The field name remained the same, the data type was still numeric, and none of the existing technical validations detected the change.

The pipeline continued running as expected, but the model was now receiving information with a different business meaning.

This brings us to an important point: Just because an AI pipeline runs successfully doesn't necessarily mean we can trust its output.

Building reliable AI systems requires us to look beyond the model itself. We need to understand where the data originates, how it changes as it moves through different systems, whether it meets quality expectations, and who is responsible when something goes wrong.

In this article, we'll explore three important elements of trustworthy AI pipelines (data quality, data lineage, and accountability) and look at how engineering teams can incorporate them into their existing workflows without making the process unnecessarily complicated.

Most modern data pipelines come with some form of operational monitoring. Engineering teams track job completion, execution time, system availability, and processing failures.

These metrics are important because they help us understand whether our systems are functioning as expected.

Operational monitoring primarily tells us whether a pipeline executed successfully. It doesn't necessarily tell us whether the data being processed is accurate, consistent, or suitable for the model consuming it.

Suppose we're building a loan risk model that uses a customer's debt-to-income ratio as one of its input features.

Debt-to-income ratio = Monthly debt payments / Monthly income

Now imagine that an upstream system starts supplying annual income instead of monthly income.

The calculation still executes successfully. The values are numeric, the transformation doesn't throw an error, and the model continues generating predictions.

However, the resulting debt-to-income ratio is incorrect because the numerator and denominator represent different time periods.

This is where traditional monitoring falls short.

To build trustworthy AI pipelines, we need to look at different dimensions of system health.

A pipeline can be operationally healthy while processing unreliable data. Similarly, a model can continue producing predictions even when the meaning of an important input field has changed.

For engineering teams, the objective should be to identify these problems as early as possible, ideally before they reach downstream models.

We've all heard the phrase "garbage in, garbage out."

And despite all the progress we've made in artificial intelligence, this principle hasn't changed.

AI models may be capable of processing enormous volumes of data and identifying complex patterns, but they cannot automatically guarantee that the information they're receiving is correct.

This is where data quality becomes important.

Data quality refers to how well information meets the requirements of its intended use. In AI pipelines, it helps us determine whether incoming data is sufficiently reliable for model training, evaluation, or inference.

Let's look at four dimensions that are particularly relevant.

Imagine we're developing a loan risk model that relies on customer income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

What happens if 20% of the incoming records are missing income information?

Should we reject those records? Should we replace missing values using an approved statistical method? Or should we flag them for additional review?

There isn't one answer that works for every system.

The right approach depends on the model, the business requirements, and the potential consequences of the decision.

What matters is that missing information is handled deliberately.

For example, replacing missing income with zero may allow the pipeline to continue running, but it could significantly distort the model's predictions.

Validity checks whether values meet expected formats, ranges, and business rules.

Consider a customer record containing the following information:

The credit utilization value immediately stands out.

Although credit utilization can exceed 100% in certain circumstances, a value of 450% may warrant investigation.

This highlights an important distinction: Not every unusual value is incorrect, and not every technically valid value is meaningful.

A database may accept any numeric value, but the business may need additional rules to determine whether that value is appropriate for the model.

Engineering teams should distinguish between invalid records, unexpected observations, and legitimate exceptions.

This is one of the most common challenges in enterprise data environments.

Imagine two systems providing customer income information.

Both datasets contain a column called income.

If we combine these datasets without understanding their definitions, we risk introducing inconsistencies into downstream calculations.

The data may look perfectly fine from a technical perspective. The problem is that the same field represents different business concepts.

This is why data definitions, units, and transformation rules are just as important as schema validation.

Suppose a model predicts a customer's current financial risk using income information that was last updated 18 months ago.

The data might be accurate, complete, and consistent.

But is it current enough to support the decision?

Different AI applications have different freshness requirements.

A real-time fraud detection model may require near-real-time transaction information, while a long-term forecasting model may work with less frequently updated datasets.

The important thing is to define these expectations based on how the data will be used.

The good news is that improving data quality doesn't always require sophisticated enterprise tools.

A practical starting point is to define validation rules for the most important input fields.

For example, consider the following conceptual configuration:

This is an illustrative data quality contract rather than executable configuration for a particular framework.

It defines basic expectations and specifies what should happen when the data fails validation.

Tools such as Great Expectations can help automate these checks. For smaller systems, custom SQL or Python validations may be sufficient.

However, technical validation alone isn't enough.

Remember our original example where the income field changed from gross to net income?

Both values could easily pass a rule requiring income to be greater than zero.

Detecting that kind of issue requires clear business definitions, communication with upstream systems, and appropriate change management.

In other words, data quality isn't just about checking values. It's also about understanding what those values represent.

Now let's assume our loan risk model generates an unexpectedly high risk score for a customer.

The model output is available, but we want to understand what contributed to the prediction.

The income information came from a customer application system. Outstanding debt came from another database. Both datasets went through several transformations before reaching the feature engineering pipeline.

The final features were then passed to the model.

At this point, a seemingly simple question becomes surprisingly difficult:

Where exactly did the information used for this prediction come from?

This is where data lineage becomes valuable.

Data lineage describes how data originates, moves, and changes across different systems.

For AI pipelines, it helps us understand the journey from raw source data to the features used by a model.

Source Systems → Data Transformation → Feature Engineering → Model Inference → Predictions

Each stage introduces dependencies that can affect downstream results.

Data lineage can be captured at different levels of detail.

Dataset-level lineage shows relationships between datasets.

Loan Applications → Cleaned Applications → Model Features

This helps us understand how datasets move through the overall architecture.

However, suppose the model's debt-to-income ratio suddenly changes.

Dataset-level lineage might tell us which datasets were involved, but it may not provide enough detail to identify the affected field.

That's where column-level lineage becomes useful.

debt_to_income_ratio = monthly_debt_payment / monthly_income

Column-level lineage can show that the resulting feature depends on two upstream attributes.

If one of those attributes changes, engineers can trace the dependency and investigate the impact.

This is especially valuable in environments where multiple reports, applications, and AI models depend on shared data sources.

Large organizations may use dedicated metadata management and lineage platforms.

However, smaller teams can start by capturing essential metadata during pipeline execution.

OpenLineage provides an open standard for collecting and exchanging lineage metadata across supported systems.

It's important to understand that lineage doesn't automatically guarantee data accuracy.

A pipeline can be perfectly documented and still contain incorrect transformation logic.

But when something goes wrong, lineage gives engineering teams a clearer starting point for investigation.

Instead of searching across multiple systems and trying to reconstruct dependencies manually, they can identify where data originated and how it changed along the way.

An AI model starts producing unexpected results.

The data science team checks the model and finds no issues.

The data engineering team confirms that the pipelines are running successfully.

The source-system team verifies that data was delivered according to its interface.

Everyone has completed their individual checks, but nobody has identified who should coordinate the investigation.

This is where accountability becomes important.

AI pipelines often involve multiple teams responsible for different stages of the data lifecycle. Without clearly defined ownership, even relatively simple issues can take longer to resolve.

A practical accountability framework should distinguish between three responsibilities.

Data owners are responsible for defining the business meaning and expected quality of critical information.

For example, someone needs to determine whether an income field represents gross income, net income, or another financial measure.

These definitions should be documented and communicated to downstream consumers.

Data engineering and platform teams typically manage data ingestion, transformations, validation mechanisms, and pipeline operations.

Their responsibilities may include implementing quality checks, monitoring failures, and assessing the technical impact of changes.

However, technical teams shouldn't be expected to make business-definition decisions without appropriate input.

Data science and ML engineering teams are responsible for evaluating model behavior, managing model versions, and assessing how changes in input data may affect predictions.

If a critical feature changes, the model team may need to determine whether additional testing, recalibration, or retraining is required.

Defining ownership is useful, but connecting it to an operational process is even more important.

Consider a critical data quality failure during feature generation.

The exact workflow will vary depending on the organization and the risk associated with the application.

The objective is to ensure that technical alerts lead to clear actions.

After all, an alert that nobody owns is just another notification waiting to be ignored.

So far, we've discussed why data quality, lineage, and accountability matter.

But how can we bring these concepts into everyday engineering practices?

Here are five controls that teams can introduce without redesigning their entire architecture.

Data contracts define expectations between data producers and consumers.

They can document schemas, field definitions, units, freshness requirements, and compatibility expectations.

For example, rather than specifying only that annual_income is numeric, a contract should clarify whether it represents gross or net income, the currency, and the applicable time period.

This reduces the risk of downstream systems misinterpreting technically valid information.

Quality gates validate critical data before it progresses through the pipeline.

These checks can be implemented during ingestion, transformation, feature generation, or inference.

For example, a feature engineering process calculating debt-to-income ratios should verify that debt and income values use compatible time periods.

Failure handling should reflect the severity of the issue. Some records may be quarantined, while more serious failures may require stopping the pipeline.

Pipeline execution should produce sufficient metadata to identify source datasets, transformations, and downstream outputs.

Where appropriate, teams should also capture model and feature versions associated with predictions.

This information supports impact analysis, debugging, and investigation when unexpected results occur.

Datasets change, transformation logic is updated, features are modified, and models are retrained.

Versioning helps engineering teams understand which components were active at a particular point in time.

Relevant evidence may include pipeline configurations, dataset snapshots, model versions, validation outcomes, and deployment records.

Every critical data element or pipeline component should have an identified owner or responsible team.

More importantly, ownership should connect directly to incident management and change approval processes.

If a source definition changes, teams should know who evaluates the impact.

If a quality gate fails, the responsible team should receive the alert.

If model performance deteriorates, the investigation should have a clear escalation path.

These controls are most effective when they become part of normal development and deployment practices rather than separate administrative activities.

Implementing comprehensive governance across an entire data environment can be challenging, particularly for organizations with legacy systems and complex dependencies.

A more effective approach is to begin with one critical AI pipeline.

For example, a team operating a loan risk model could start by identifying the inputs that have the greatest influence on its predictions.

These might include income, outstanding debt, repayment history, and credit utilization.

For each critical input, the team can document five things:

Once these foundations are established, the team can implement automated checks and gradually extend the approach to additional datasets.

This incremental strategy also makes it easier to demonstrate the value of governance controls.

For instance, teams can track how quickly data-related incidents are detected, how long investigations take, and whether recurring issues are reduced.

The goal isn't to introduce governance for its own sake.

It's to improve the reliability, maintainability, and transparency of the systems developers are responsible for operating.

Explainable AI has become an important topic in machine learning.

Techniques such as feature importance analysis and SHAP can help teams understand which inputs influence model predictions.

However, explainability and data trustworthiness address different problems.

Suppose a model explanation identifies debt-to-income ratio as a major contributor to a customer's high-risk classification.

That explanation may accurately describe the model's behavior.

But if the debt-to-income ratio was calculated using an incorrectly defined income field, the explanation alone may not reveal the underlying data issue.

This highlights the importance of evaluating AI systems across multiple dimensions.

Model explainability helps us understand how predictions are generated.

Data quality helps establish whether inputs satisfy defined expectations.

Data lineage provides visibility into where information originated and how it was transformed.

Accountability ensures that identified problems can be investigated and addressed.

These capabilities are complementary rather than interchangeable.

None independently guarantees that an AI system is accurate, fair, secure, or compliant. Together, however, they provide a stronger foundation for evaluating and improving system reliability.

As AI systems become more integrated into business processes, engineering teams face increasing expectations around reliability, transparency, and accountability.

Model accuracy and operational performance remain essential, but they represent only part of the overall picture.

A pipeline can execute successfully while processing inconsistent information. A model can generate predictions using features whose definitions have changed. And an explanation can describe a model's behavior without identifying problems in the underlying data.

Building trustworthy AI therefore requires attention to the entire data lifecycle.

Data quality controls help detect unreliable inputs. Lineage provides visibility into how information moves through systems. Clear ownership ensures that issues can be investigated and resolved.

Importantly, these practices don't need to begin with large-scale governance programs or expensive technology investments.

Engineering teams can start with a single critical pipeline, identify its most important data elements, establish quality expectations, and introduce basic traceability and accountability mechanisms.

Over time, these practices can become part of standard development and deployment workflows.

The real measure of a trustworthy AI pipeline isn't simply whether it produces a prediction. It's whether the organization can understand, validate, and take responsibility for the information behind that prediction.

After all, a green dashboard is reassuring. But it shouldn't be the only evidence that an AI system is working as intended.

#10177. How to Use Transformers.js in a Chrome Extension

We recently released a Transformers.js demo browser extension powered by Gemma 4 E2B to help users navigate the web.

While building it, we ran into several practical observations about Manifest V3 runtimes, model loading, and messaging that are worth sharing.

This guide is for developers who want to run local AI features in a Chrome extension with Transformers.js under Manifest V3 constraints.

By the end, you will have the same architecture used in this project: a background service worker that hosts models, a side panel chat UI, and a content script for page-level actions.

In this guide, we will recreate the core architecture of Transformers.js Gemma 4 Browser Assistant, using the published extension as a reference and the open-source codebase as the implementation map.

Before diving in, a quick scope note: I will not go deep on the React UI layer or Vite build configuration. The focus here is the high-level architecture decisions: what runs in each Chrome runtime and how those pieces are orchestrated.

If Manifest V3 is new to you, read this short overview first: What is Manifest V3?.

In MV3, your architecture starts in public/manifest.json. This project defines three entry points:

The background service worker also handles chrome.action.onClicked to open the side panel for the active tab. Related entry point to know: a popup can be defined with action.default_popup and works well for quick actions. This project uses a side panel for persistent chat, but the orchestration pattern is the same.

The key design decision is to keep heavy orchestration in the background and keep UI/page logic thin.

One practical consequence of this division is that the conversation history also lives in background (Agent.chatMessages): the UI sends events like AGENT_GENERATE_TEXT, background appends the message, runs inference, then emits MESSAGES_UPDATE back to the side panel.

This split avoids duplicate model loads, keeps the UI responsive, and respects Chrome's security boundaries around DOM access.

Once runtimes are separated, messaging becomes the backbone. In this project, all messages are typed through enums in src/shared/types.ts.

The orchestration rule is simple: the background is the single coordinator; side panel and content script are specialized workers that request actions and render results.

In src/shared/constants.ts, this extension uses two model roles:

The split is intentional: Gemma 4 handles reasoning/tool decisions, while MiniLM generates vector embeddings for the semantic similarity search in ask_website and find_history.

All inference runs in background (src/background/background.ts):

This gives a single model host for all tabs/sessions, avoids duplicate memory usage, and keeps the side panel UI responsive. Because models are loaded from the background service worker, artifacts are cached under the extension origin (chrome-extension://) rather than per-website origins, which gives one shared cache for the whole extension install.

MV3 lifecycle note: service workers can be suspended and restarted, so model runtime state should be treated as recoverable and re-initialized when needed.

Why keep this narrow: permissions define user trust and Chrome Web Store review risk. Request only what your features actually need, and state clearly that inference runs locally in the extension runtime so users understand where their data is processed.

Before the execution loop, it helps to understand how model tool calling works (the basis for any agentic workflow). You pass messages plus a tool schema (name, description, and parameters), and Transformers.js formats the actual prompt from those inputs using the model's chat template. Because chat templates are model-specific, the exact tool-call format depends on the model you use. With Gemma-4-style templates, the model emits a special tool-call token block when it decides to call one.

At generation time, the model can emit output like:

That is exactly why this project has a normalization layer (webMcp) and a parser (extractToolCalls): model output must be converted into deterministic tool executions.

src/background/agent/webMcp.tsx normalizes extension tools into a model-friendly shape:

Example tools include get_open_tabs, go_to_tab, open_url, close_tab, find_history, ask_website, and highlight_website_element.

The core design choice here is to separate internal model messages from UI-facing chat messages:

This keeps user communication clean while preserving a deterministic tool loop in the background.

State placement is another architectural decision that matters a lot in MV3. In this implementation, state is split by lifecycle and access pattern:

As described in section 1.2, keeping conversation history in background gives one canonical state across UI updates. This keeps short-lived state in memory, durable settings in extension storage, and heavy retrieval data in a local database.

You do not need a complex build setup, but MV3 does require predictable outputs for each runtime.

The goal is simple: one artifact per Chrome entry point, in the exact place public/manifest.json expects.

The architecture choice that unlocks this whole project is clear separation of concerns: background owns orchestration and model execution, UI surfaces stay thin, and content scripts handle page access.

This project uses a side panel, but the same approach works for other setups:

The practical rule is simple: decide where state lives (global, tabId, or site-scoped), keep that state and the model inference in background (basically as background services), and let UI/content runtimes act as focused clients.

#10176. Kagi, the paid Google Search alternative, now has a Gmail rival too

Kagi is best known as a paid alternative to Google Search, but the company is now introducing its own email service that offers an alternative to Gmail.

Kagi Mail has been in the works for a long time, the company says in a post today, but it’s only just now launching in public beta. Users get an “@kagimail.com” address or can use their own domain, with both email and a calendar included.

There’s a 60-day trial for Kagi Mail, with the service costing $99.99/year (or included in Kagi’s $25/month Ultimate plan). The reason you’d pay that, Kagi explains, is because this is a product designed to “do its job and then get out of your way,” with no ads or “surveillance” as a part of the package.

Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.

For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.

There’s a mobile app coming for Kagi Mail in early 2027, with a contact book and Kagi Assistant integration also slated for early next year. There is some natural language AI for organization, blocking of tracking pixels and remote images by default, and support for email clients like Apple Mail, and Kagi says everything can be exported to move to another provider should you choose.

#10175. Google Maps might change its colors again, but it’s optional this time [Gallery]

Google Maps has a pretty consistent style, but a new option appears to be in the works with a darker “high-visibility” setting.

The last major change to Google Maps styling came in 2023 (yes, time flies) when the platform rolled out a new color palette to all users. This was divisive among users, but ultimately worked out.

Now, Google appears to be working on another new shake-up.

The folks over at Android Authority spotted a new “high-visibility” toggle in the latest Google Maps update for Android, with the new style having darker colors for the map in both light and dark modes, as well as a purple line for your route compared to the blue we’re used to seeing.

The change was also spotted on Android Auto, with much darker colors (including a near-black dark mode) in both color settings for your car’s display. This is likely tied to this new “High-visibility” setting, but it’s hard to say for certain – teardowns and enabling new features early can only tell us so much.

This appears to all be controlled by a new “Map style” setting in Google Maps, with “Standard” and “High-visibility” settings available. Functionally, everything remains the same, it’s just a new set of colors.

So, where the previous color changes were forced on all users, this one is at least optional, and the “High-visibility” naming seems like it’s targeted at those with difficulties in sight more so than just a general change for all users.

#10174. On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery

Today, we are introducing on-device Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities in Google AI Edge Gallery. Voice is often the most natural way to interact with AI on phones and wearables. Recent advances in compact speech architectures now make it possible to run accurate, multilingual ASR and expressive TTS models entirely on device, all within a small memory footprint, with low latency, and completely offline. By pairing these lightweight speech models with on-device small language models (SLMs) like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4, developers can build apps that stream live transcriptions as the user speaks and synthesize natural spoken replies locally.

This release brings together major advancements across both Google’s system speech models and the open-weight ecosystem:

Below, we’ll explore how this local voice pipeline powers the new XR (Extended Reality) Language Teacher showcase, upgrades AI Chat in Google AI Edge Gallery, and how you can build with these APIs and models today.

Learning a language while traveling happens in the real world, often in underground stations, busy markets, or abroad where Wi-Fi and roaming data may not be available. To show how vision, language, and speech models can work together 100% locally on your phone with no network connection needed, we built the XR Language Teacher showcase in Google AI Edge Gallery. Simply point your camera at an unfamiliar object or menu, ask "What is that, and how do I ask for one?", and immediately hear an explanation in your language alongside authentic pronunciation in the local language.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

With inference running locally on a paired phone, the same experience works standalone on a phone and extends naturally to hands-free smart glasses. To see how we adapted Language Teacher for intelligent glasses check out our recent talk at Android Dev Summit: Building Audio-First Experiences for Intelligent Eyewear with Gemini Nano.

Beyond the XR Language Teacher showcase, we also built ASR and TTS directly into Google AI Edge Gallery’s main AI Chat feature, giving on-device SLMs like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 a natural, offline voice interface while on the go.

Link to Youtube Video (visible only when JS is disabled)

While multimodal models like Gemma 4 can process audio inputs directly, we provide a modular solution for cascading language models with separate, lightweight voice models for latency optimization and flexibility. Depending on your target devices and model requirements, our open-source code on GitHub shows you the optimized and recommended solution for Android using ML Kit, as well as MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform coverage and open model support.

For developers building for Android devices, ML Kit’s GenAI Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech APIs provide a standardized, platform-integrated path out of the box. With the underlying speech models managed through AICore and Google’s on-device speech services, developers get production-grade quality without having to manage model downloads or worry about APK size bloat. Your app also benefits automatically from hardware acceleration across NPU and TPU backends (when available) and seamless background model updates.

Integrating ASR and TTS into cross-platform applications usually requires handling low-level audio framing, Voice Activity Detection (VAD), and complex decoding pipelines. MediaPipe Task simplifies this by providing unified, turnkey ASR and TTS APIs across iOS, macOS, Windows, Linux, and Web that abstract away manual pre-processing, audio stream routing, and platform-specific audio management into simple, high-level interfaces:

Under the hood, ML Kit and MediaPipe Tasks are powered by LiteRT, Google’s high-performance on-device AI inference infrastructure. Cross-platform applications requiring even more fine-grained control over speech processing or custom model architectures can also build on it directly.

Speech models often rely on multiple subgraphs and auxiliary assets, such as encoder/decoder subgraphs and tokenizers for ASR, or phonemizer dictionaries, voice embeddings, and vocoders for TTS. All required components for each model are packaged into a single .litertlm file for easy deployment. The app ships with ready-to-use .litertlm models, including Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 (multilingual ASR), PocketTTS 100M (multilingual TTS), Phonon 31M (ultra-lightweight English TTS), and Kokoro-82M (multilingual TTS). Beyond these, the vibrant Hugging Face LiteRT Community with over 10K+ followers offers a growing catalog of open-weight models, like Whisper, Qwen3-ASR and Moonshine for ASR, or Qwen3-TTS and Matcha for TTS. For developers seeking custom implementations or support for additional open-weight voice models, LiteRT provides a rich set of multimodal model examples to help you get started, with more on the way.

Adding a local voice pipeline takes on-device SLMs beyond typing-based chat interfaces, enabling natural, voice-first interactions that work anywhere, completely offline. All the building blocks to try these experiences or integrate them into your own apps are available today:

We'd like to extend a special thanks to our significant contributors for their work on this project:

Alice Zheng, Ajay Dudani, Alex Kanaukou, Amy Zeppenfeld, Byungchul Kim, Cheng Yang, Chintan Parikh, Chris Parsons, Cormac Brick, David Chou, Dong Chen, Geonsun Lee, Glenn Cameron, Hriday Chhabria, Ian Ballantyne, Ireneu Pla, James O’Donnell, Jamieson Pryor, Jason Poon, Jenn Lee, Jianing Wei, Jing Jin, Jingxiao Zheng, Jingyu Shi, Karthik Thirumalai, Kristen Wright, Lu Wang, Marius Kintel, Matthias Grundmann, Miao Wang, Mogan Shieh, Na Li, Paul Hsia, Qiumin Xu, Ravi Shankar, Rishika Sinha, Ronald Wotzlaw, Sachin Kotwani, Sandeep Patil, Sebastian Schmidt, Shao-Fu Shih, Shuangfeng Li, Suril Shah, Tiger Souvannakoumane, Tzu-Ping Chen, Weiyi Wang, Wentao Tu, Yang Yang, Yi-Chun Kuo, Yishuang Pang, Yu-che Liu, Yu-hui Chen, Yuling Liang, Zhihao Yang, Zichuan Wei.

#10173. DeepSeek-V4: a million-token context that agents can actually use

DeepSeek released V4 today. Two MoE checkpoints are on the Hub: DeepSeek-V4-Pro at 1.6T total parameters with 49B active, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash at 284B total with 13B active. Both have a 1M-token context window. The benchmark numbers are competitive, but not SOTA. It doesn't matter. The real innovation is how DeepSeek v4 is designed for efficient large context length support, and hence as one of the best candidates for agentic tasks.

Focusing on long running agentic workloads. Running a frontier open model as an agent today breaks in predictable ways. The model stops. You reprompt. The trace blows past the context budget, or the KV cache fills the GPU, or tool-call round trips degrade halfway through a long task. V4 is built to fix these known failures, and point the way for the community to follow.

This post covers three things: what the architecture does differently to make long-context inference cheap, the agent-specific post-training decisions that compound on top of it, and some takeaways from the paper that help reason about these changes.

A 1M context window is just capacity, not performance. Whether you can use it depends on the cost of every forward pass at that depth. For an agent running a long tool-use trajectory (a SWE-bench task, a multi-step browse session, a terminal session with hundreds of commands), every tool result is appended to the context, and every subsequent token pays the full attention cost against everything that came before.

Two numbers matter: single-token inference FLOPs and KV cache size. Both grow with sequence length. At 1M tokens, DeepSeek-V4-Pro requires 27% of single-token inference FLOPs compared with DeepSeek-V3.2, so it runs faster on the same hardware. It also uses 10% of the KV cache memory. V4-Flash drops these numbers even further: 10% of the FLOPs and 7% of the KV cache.

If we compare the KV cache memory against a established architecture like grouped query attention with 8 heads, stored in the usual bfloat16 format, DeepSeek v4 requires roughly 2% the cache size. This makes it much easier to deploy for very large context handling.

Figure 1: benchmark comparison (left), per-token FLOPs and accumulated KV cache against sequence length (right).

The efficiency gain comes from splitting attention into two mechanisms and interleaving them across layers.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) compresses KV entries by 4x along the sequence dimension using softmax-gated pooling with a learned positional bias. A lightning indexer (FP4, ReLU-scored multi-head dot product) picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. It inherits the sparse-selection idea from DeepSeek Sparse Attention in V3.2, but runs it over blocks that are already 4x shorter than the original sequence. The indexer's search space shrinks with it.

Figure 3: CSA. The compressor collapses every 4 tokens into one compressed KV entry. The lightning indexer picks the top-k compressed blocks per query. A sliding-window branch handles the most recent uncompressed tokens.

Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) compresses KV entries by 128x and drops the sparse selection. Every query attends densely to every compressed block. The compressed sequence is short enough that dense attention is cheap.

Figure 4: HCA. A heavier compressor (128x vs. 4x) followed by dense attention over the compressed stream, with the same sliding-window branch for recency.

The layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Different layers carry different attention patterns, and forcing one mechanism across all of them wastes capacity. In V4-Pro's 61-layer stack, layers 0–1 are HCA, layers 2–60 alternate CSA and HCA, and the MTP block at the end runs sliding-window only.

Both paths use FP8 storage for most KV entries and BF16 only for the RoPE dimensions. The lightning indexer inside CSA runs in FP4. These storage choices compound with the compression ratios to produce the 2% KV cache figure.

Figure 2: overall architecture. Attention layers alternate between CSA and HCA. Feed-forward layers use DeepSeekMoE. Residual connections are replaced with manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC).

Efficient long-context attention is necessary for agent workflows but not sufficient. The paper describes three post-training and infrastructure choices that target agent use cases directly.

V3.2 kept reasoning traces across tool-result rounds but discarded them whenever a new user message arrived. For an agent handling a single user turn, this was fine. For multi-turn agentic workflows, where the user sends a follow-up after the agent has already chained several tool calls, the model lost its accumulated reasoning and had to reconstruct state.

V4 preserves reasoning content across user message boundaries when the conversation contains tool calls. The model retains the complete reasoning history across all rounds, including across user turns. This allows a coherent, cumulative chain of thought over long-horizon agent tasks. For conversational use without tools, the old behavior is preserved: reasoning is flushed on each turn to keep context concise.

Figure 7: thinking with tools (top) preserves reasoning across all turns. Thinking without tools (bottom) discards reasoning at each new user message.

V4 introduces a |DSML| special token and an XML-based tool-call format. The XML format reduces escaping failures compared to JSON-in-string tool calls, a common failure mode when models emit nested quoted content.

The schema separates string parameters (passed as-is with string="true") from structured parameters (passed as JSON with string="false"). This removes a class of parsing errors around numbers and booleans that JSON tool-call formats routinely hit.

The agent behavior was trained with RL against real tool environments. The paper describes the sandbox infrastructure built for that purpose. DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec) is a Rust platform that exposes four execution substrates behind one Python SDK: function calls, containers, microVMs (Firecracker), and full VMs (QEMU). A single cluster runs hundreds of thousands of concurrent sandboxes.

Three DSec features matter for agent training: fast image loading via layered 3FS storage (so RL rollouts do not wait on container startup), preemption-safe trajectory replay (so interrupted training steps resume without re-running tool calls), and a uniform API across substrates (so training harnesses target function calls or full VMs without rewriting). These infrastructure decisions underpin the agent benchmark scores.

The knowledge and reasoning numbers are competitive but not leading. The agent numbers are where V4-Pro-Max separates from the field.

Specific numbers from the agent section of Table 6:

In the paper's internal R&D coding benchmark, 30 curated tasks across PyTorch, CUDA, Rust, and C++, V4-Pro-Max hits 67% pass rate, versus 47% for Sonnet 4.5 and 70% for Opus 4.5. In a survey of 85 DeepSeek developers using V4-Pro as their daily driver, 52% said it was ready to replace their current primary coding model and 39% leaned toward yes.

The long-context retrieval numbers are in Figure 9. MRCR 8-needle accuracy stays above 0.82 through 256K tokens and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Figure 9: MRCR 8-needle retrieval. V4-Pro-Max stays above 0.82 through 256K and holds at 0.59 at 1M.

Four checkpoints are on the Hub. The instruct models use FP4 for MoE expert weights and FP8 for everything else. The base models are FP8 throughout.

Both instruct models support three reasoning modes: Non-think (fast, no chain of thought), Think High (explicit reasoning in blocks), and Think Max (maximum reasoning effort with a dedicated system prompt). Think Max requires a context window of at least 384K tokens. The recommended sampling parameters across all modes are temperature=1.0, top_p=1.0.

The V4-Pro numbers on SWE Verified, MCPAtlas, and the internal R&D benchmark put it at parity with frontier closed models on agent tasks. The open question is how the community's tool harnesses adapt to the |DSML| schema and whether the interleaved thinking gains transfer to out-of-domain agent frameworks.

Figures in this blog post are from the technical report at DeepSeek_V4.pdf.

According to my personal tests DeepSeek V4 Flash (Non-thinking mode) passed the Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval test on both 32k and 435k actual prompt tokens with a 100% result across depths of 0-100%. In no-needle negative control with the NOT_FOUND instruction, the model also returned 100% correct failures, reducing the risk of contamination and false positives.

So thinking mode may degrade behaviour in some tests.

#10171. How Developers Can Detect Fake Payment Gateways and Build Secure Checkout Integrations

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

However, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

Fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

For developers, understanding these risks is important when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

These techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The important distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

An attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The important part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

Developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:

The verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

The example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another important issue in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:

The example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

A well-designed checkout integration should verify every important transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

#10170. Hands-on: Sony’s Walkman-revival USB-C headphones are back in stock and worth a look

Sony’s iconic Walkman headphones are back in the USB-C MDR-3R and, after quickly selling out on launch day, they’ve now been restocked. And, after using them, I can see why they sold out so quickly.

The MDR-3R are Sony’s revival of the wired over-ear headphones that many used with a classic Walkman player. The retro style still looks great in 2026, but using an original pair is a bit of a headache in today’s age of headphone jack-less smartphones. So it was nice to see Sony give this a revival with USB-C.

Update 11/24: After we first published our hands-on with MDR-3R last week, Sony’s USB-C headphones sold out pretty quickly again. As of today, though, they’re back in stock and still shipping in early December – don’t miss out!

While the style won’t be for everyone, I think these work brilliantly. The sound quality is excellent and having a pair of headphones that doesn’t fully enclose my ears is pretty refreshing. There’s no noise cancellation, but with open-ear earbuds becoming more popular, I actually really like these as a similar solution (though high volumes will definitely be heard by those around you). I’m not fully cut off from the world around me, but I’m also able to get good sound quality. Lows are the weakness here, with unimpressive bass drops, but the sound quality is crisp and clear and pretty neutral, and the open-ish style makes it feel like the room around me is filled with music.

The physical hardware is great. While a plastic and metal build is objectively not as comfy as a premium pair of ANC headphones, the extremely light weight helps MDR-3R become an afterthought. You simply forget you’re wearing them after a few minutes.

The earpads are swappable, with orange and blue options included in the box.

As for the USB-C cable, it’s fully plug-and-play. No app needed and it worked across every device I tested (including Pixel, which doesn’t work with all USB-C audio output). I do wish the cable was perhaps a few inches longer, but it’s long enough to wear the headphones with my phone in my front pocket. There’s a remote along the cable for play/pause and volume adjustments, though I think it’s a little too high on the cable.

For $59.99, these are a fun pair of USB-C headphones to have on hand. They sound good, work great, and don’t cost an arm and a leg. I can see why they sold out so quickly on launch day – in just 10 hours, Sony told me.

Sony MDR-3R are back in stock now and shipping in early December. If you want a pair, I say don’t wait. They’re well worth at least trying if you can get them for retail price – please don’t give in to the scalpers selling these at double, they’re not worth that.

#10169. How to build scalable web apps with OpenAI's Privacy Filter

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

User problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

What gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:

Note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:

User problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

What gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:

The frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, new-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

User problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :

A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:

@server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client users hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

One gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

#10166. Introducing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni: Long-Context Multimodal Intelligence for Documents, Audio and Video Agents

Benchmark highlightsBuilding on Nemotron Nano V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers substantial visual gains and adds entirely new audio and video+audio capabilities - while also leading another open-weights omni model, Qwen3-Omni, in many domains.

Efficiency highlightsCompared to other open omni models with the same interactivity, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers 7.4x higher system efficiency for multi-document use cases and 9.2x higher system efficiency for video use cases Figure 1. Total system throughput for multi-document and video use cases sustained by each model at a fixed per‑user interactivity threshold (tokens/sec/user)

At a high level, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is aimed at five classes of workloads:

This is not only about OCR. The model is positioned for long, messy, high-value documents where understanding depends on layout, tables, figures, formulas, section structure, and cross-page references. Think contracts, technical papers, reports, manuals, multi-page forms, or compliance packets. The model can handle 100+ page documents.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni includes strong speech understanding capabilities that enable high-quality transcription across diverse audio conditions. It handles long-form audio with varying speakers, accents, and background noise. These capabilities can be integrated into broader workflows, allowing spoken content to be transcribed, analyzed, and combined with other modalities for tasks like summarization, question answering, and cross-modal reasoning.

Many enterprise and developer workflows depend on mixed audio and visual evidence: screen recordings with narration, training videos, meetings with slides, tutorials, product demos, customer support captures, and long-form video archives. Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is built to reason over those inputs jointly.

The Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model is specifically trained for agentic computer use, enabling it to assist with tasks in graphical user interface (GUI) environments. Its capabilities include interpreting screenshots, monitoring the state of the user interface, grounding its reasoning in on-screen visuals, and helping with action selection or workflow automation.

The model is designed for more than perception. It excels at reasoning-intensive tasks that require synthesizing information across long context windows, multiple modalities, and structured or semi-structured evidence. It can carry out multi-step reasoning, perform calculations, and connect signals from text, images, tables, and other inputs to arrive at coherent, well-supported answers.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a unified encoder-projector-decoder design. The language backbone is Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, paired with the C-RADIOv4-H vision encoder and the Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 audio encoder. The modality-specific encoders connect into the LLM backbone through lightweight projectors.

Figure 2. Model architecture of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B

The model backbone interleaves three key components: 23 Mamba selective state-space layers for efficient long-context processing; 23 MoE layers with 128 experts, top-6 routing, and a shared expert for conditional capacity; and 6 grouped-query attention layers to preserve strong global interaction and expressivity.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni combines state-space models, attention, and MoE in a unified design that maintains strong reasoning performance while remaining practical for long, multimodal contexts.

On the vision side, the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni replaces the tiling strategy used in the v2 model with dynamic resolution processing at native aspect ratio. Each image can be represented using a variable number of 16 x 16 patches, with a minimum of 1,024 to a maximum of 13,312 visual patches per image. For square images, this is equivalent to 512 x 512 and 1840 x 1840, respectively.

That flexibility is critical for handling high-resolution, complex visual inputs such as OCR-heavy documents, financial tables, slides, research figures, screenshots, and GUI layouts—especially when both fine details and overall structure need to be understood together.

For video, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a dedicated Conv3D tubelet embedding path. Instead of embedding each frame independently, every pair of consecutive frames is fused into a single "tubelet" before the ViT, halving the number of vision tokens the language model has to attend to. This allows us to either double the number of frames with the same token budget, or halve the number of tokens with the same number of frames

EVS is an important feature, enabled during inference time, that drops redundant video tokens after the vision encoder. This reduces latency and improves throughput while maintaining accuracy. The first frame of the video is kept entirely, then for each subsequent frame, EVS keeps the “dynamic” tokens where the video is changing and drops the “static” ones where nothing has changed from the previous frame. We combine this with Conv3D to enable superior compression: Conv3D fuses tokens from pairs of frames into one, and then EVS prunes redundant static information.

The audio side is powered by Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2, connected to the backbone through its own 2-layer MLP projector. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz, and the model is trained with inputs up to 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), while the LLM max context length supports 5+ hours.

This represents a shift from traditional VLM pipelines by enabling native audio processing within a shared multimodal sequence, allowing audio, visual, and text tokens to be jointly modeled. This is crucial for scenarios like narrated screen recordings, video Q&A where speech alters visual meaning, long-form instructional or meeting content, and tasks requiring temporally grounded multimodal reasoning.

Each encoder is connected to the LLM with a lightweight 2-layer MLP projector that maps encoder features into the shared embedding space. Once projected, vision, audio, and text tokens are interleaved and processed jointly.

This design keeps the overall system modular while still enabling genuine cross-modal reasoning inside the backbone itself.

The SFT stages are trained on NVIDIA H100, scaling from 32 to 128 nodes depending on the stage. The stack uses Megatron-LM, Transformer Engine, and Megatron Energon, with tensor parallelism, expert parallelism, sequence parallelism, context parallelism for the long context stages, online sequence packing, and selective activation recomputation.

Post-SFT reinforcement learning uses NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym with a Megatron backend. The RL infrastructure used a Ray-based distributed setup across B200 and H100 clusters, plus multimodal deduplication, so repeated rollouts do not multiply image, video, and audio memory.

We open-source substantial parts of our training code.

We introduce multi-environment text and omni training in Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. Our text RL training stage happens across diverse environments in Nemo-Gym, which evaluates the model’s ability to perform sequences of actions such as tool calling, writing code, and multi-part planning that satisfy the verifiable criteria.

Omni RL trains the model to reason across images, video, audio, and text within a unified framework, covering tasks from single-modality to fully multimodal scenarios. A diverse verifier suite evaluates outputs across formats like multiple-choice, math, GUI grounding, and ASR, while intentionally including unanswerable cases to teach the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient rather than hallucinate.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is trained on an enhanced dataset that emphasizes high-quality reasoning across multiple modalities. We significantly expand task coverage and introduce synthetic data for complex reasoning scenarios where public datasets are limited. To support this, we build task-specific, multi-stage pipelines for scalable synthetic data generation.

As one example, we generated approximately 11.4M synthetic QA pairs (~45B tokens) from a large corpus of real-world PDFs using NeMo Data Designer. This dataset is used to strengthen long-context document reasoning during post-training and delivers a 2.19× improvement in overall accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc.

We detail the full pipeline evolution, including failure analysis and key lessons learned, in our Data Designer developer note. The note also includes nine runnable pipeline recipes that can serve as starting points for building your own document-understanding datasets.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni can analyze and reason over long documents such as financial reports, academic papers, product manuals, etc. The following example retrieves financial metrics across a 100+ page document to calculate another metric:

Figure 3: Stylized example from the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark

The model is capable of long-context retrieval, structured extraction, table/chart reading and multi-page reasoning all in one go.

Nemotron-3 Nano Omni performs joint audio-visual analysis, both locally for specific scenes and globally across the entire video. This enables it to answer complex questions that require cross-modal reasoning—such as identifying specific visuals shown exactly when a certain topic is mentioned in the audio.

Nemotron 3 Omni can be integrated into agentic computer-use systems to reason over user intents, analyze GUI elements, and execute actions to accomplish tasks.
