#10145. What to get right before you ship webhooks

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Cursor are all sending webhooks now, and all four built them on Standard Webhooks, the open spec written by Svix. Downloads of the spec's npm package went from 1.7 million a month in September 2025 to 220 million a month currently.

This may be boring to hear for the nth time, but the reason is agents. An individual person checks on a running job a few times. An agent told to watch for changes checks every resource, every minute, for as long as it runs, and almost every one of those requests comes back with nothing new. An agent that starts a job, polls until it finishes, and then starts the next one spends most of its time waiting: six steps with 15 seconds of polling each add 90 seconds, even when every operation is fast. Polling more often adds load, and polling less often adds delay, so there's not really a sweet spot.

An event-driven API gets rid of that trade-off. It tells consumers when something changed or finished, so they stop asking. That matters most for work that runs for minutes or hours, like batch inference, fine-tuning, and video generation, and many APIs still don't offer it. Of the 57 AI APIs with long-running jobs that Svix reviewed for its State of Webhooks 2027 report, 19 make you poll for the result.

Webhooks are how most APIs push those events, and you can get a v1 out pretty fast. Making it dependable is an infrastructure problem, which is a class of problem that requires more time by default. Before you ship webhooks, you need an append-only event log behind every delivery, a fixed event format, signed payloads, retries with backoff, event IDs receivers can deduplicate on, per-endpoint isolation, and delivery logs your customers can read. If you skip one of these things, a customer is just going to bring it up later.

Each section below covers one of them with adaptable code, and Standard Webhooks works with existing verification libraries in most languages.

If the request handler that changes the data also sends the webhook, a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses the event, and nothing records that it should have gone out. A customer whose endpoint was down for longer than your retry window has no way to find out what they missed.

Both problems go away if you write each event to an append-only table, scoped per customer, in the same transaction as the change. Webhooks are delivered from that table, and the same table backs an HTTP endpoint customers can read from a cursor. Svix calls this design POKE (Publish Once, Kickoff Everywhere). Build the log first: a consumer who misses a webhook needs somewhere to resume from.

Every code path that changes state calls one helper inside its own transaction:

Pass the helper the transaction handle. An insert through the connection pool commits separately, so you can end up with the event and no change, or the change and no event.

The advisory lock prevents a subtler bug. Postgres assigns sequence values at insert time, but rows only become visible at commit. With two concurrent writers, a reader can see ID 102, store it as its cursor, and then never see ID 101 when the slower transaction commits. Holding a per-customer lock until commit makes each customer's events visible in ID order.

Reading the log is one indexed range query. The endpoint returns a cursor even when there are no new events, so a client can always store it and ask again later:

authenticate stands in for the middleware that already protects your API and sets req.customerId. That scoping stops one customer from reading another's events. A customer who was offline for a week asks for events after their last cursor and gets everything they missed, in order. Publish your retention period, since it limits how far back that works. The same log can also serve synthetic created events for existing records when a new integration needs to load its initial state.

Customers write handlers against your payloads, so you'll be supporting every field you ship.

Give each event an id, type, timestamp, and data. Use the log row's ID as the event ID so webhooks and the pull endpoint agree. Name types as a resource plus a past-tense action, like invoice.paid, and publish a catalog with an example payload for each type.

Emit an event for each state change a consumer would otherwise poll for. Deletions are the ones teams forget most. Long-running jobs need completion and failure events, such as export.completed and export.failed.

Adding a field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks handlers, so ship a new type such as invoice.paid.v2 and keep sending the old one until customers have moved over.

Anyone who finds a customer's webhook URL can POST a fake invoice.paid to it. A signature lets the receiver confirm the request came from you, wasn't modified in transit, and isn't an old request being replayed.

Standard Webhooks signs the string id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256, using a separate secret for each endpoint. Including the timestamp is what lets receivers reject old requests. Generate secrets with "whsec_" + crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64").

Send the result in three headers. The ID comes from the log and stays the same on every retry. The timestamp is the time of the current attempt, so each retry gets a new signature.

Receivers need the matching check, so put it in your docs:

The function takes the raw body because frameworks that parse JSON and serialize it again change the bytes, and the signature stops matching. It compares with crypto.timingSafeEqual, since === returns faster on an early mismatch and leaks timing information. It rejects requests more than five minutes old to block replays. The signature header is a space-separated list so that during a secret rotation you can send one signature per secret and the receiver accepts either.

That code shows how the scheme works. In production, use a Standard Webhooks library on both ends. It implements the same algorithm:

Receiving endpoints go down during deploys and outages, and they return errors when they're rate limited. If you only try once, each of those is a lost webhook.

Count any non-2xx response as a failure, redirects included. Following a redirect to an arbitrary host is a security problem in its own right. Count slow responses as failures too. The code below gives up after 15 seconds. Publish whatever limit you pick, because customer handlers have to respond within it.

These delays match the schedule Svix runs in production: eight attempts over a little more than 27 hours. The early retries cover restarts. The later ones give someone time to notice an outage and fix it. After each failure, pass the number of attempts so far to nextAttemptAt, and when it returns null, mark the delivery as failed. The event is still in the log, so once the customer fixes their server they can replay it or read it from the pull endpoint.

Store attempt state in a table next to the log. Timers in process memory disappear when the process restarts, and you don't need a message broker to avoid that.

Decide what happens to endpoints that never come back. Svix disables an endpoint after five days of continuous failure and emits an event so the sender can tell the customer. Pick your own threshold, notify the customer when you disable their endpoint, and let them turn it back on.

Retries mean some events arrive twice. Usually the receiver processed the event but timed out before you saw its response, so you sent it again. Senders accept this at-least-once behavior because the alternative is dropping events, and receivers handle the duplicates.

Receivers deduplicate on webhook-id, which doesn't change between retries. The insert that stores the event can also be the duplicate check:

webhook_inbox needs a text primary key id and a jsonb column payload. The handler verifies the signature, stores the event, and returns 204. A background worker processes the inbox, so the handler responds well within the sender's timeout. express.raw gives the route the unparsed body that verification needs.

Put this pattern in your docs with a note about ordering. Events in the log have a fixed order, but webhook deliveries don't always arrive in it. A retried invoice.created can land after invoice.paid. Receivers should keep whichever event has the newer updated_at, or read the pull endpoint when they need strict ordering.

With a shared worker pool, one customer's hanging endpoint can tie up every worker for the full timeout while other customers' events wait. Limit concurrent deliveries per endpoint, and slow down delivery to endpoints that keep failing.

Customer-supplied URLs are also an attack surface. Someone can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal hostname and get your servers to call your cloud metadata service or private network. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). Resolve the hostname before connecting, reject private and loopback addresses, and don't follow redirects. The delivery code sets redirect: "manual" for this reason.

Without a self-serve view, every "did you send it?" question goes to an engineer who has to search logs.

Give customers a page to add and remove endpoints, choose event types, and rotate secrets. For each message, show every attempt with its timestamp, status code, and response body. The response body usually contains the customer's own error message. Add buttons to replay a failed message and to send a test event.

Expose the same operations in your API. Creating an endpoint and choosing its event types should take one authenticated request, because scripts and AI agents now set up a lot of integrations and can't click through a dashboard.

This is the biggest item here because it needs a UI, and it's the one teams most often leave out of the first release.

You can build all of this yourself, and many teams have. It comes down to the fact that it's cheap to manage delivery for 99% of your webhooks, but it's nontrivial to guarantee it for 100% of them. This is also ignoring the UX side such as offering the customer portal for your customers to manage their webhooks in.

Svix, which sponsored this article, handles webhook delivery. You keep the event log and decide what goes in it. A small relay reads new rows and passes each one to Svix:

Svix also hosts the debugging portal. This call returns a single-use link where the customer can manage endpoints, read delivery logs, and replay messages:

The free tier includes 50,000 messages a month and doesn't require a credit card.

Before the first customer registers an endpoint, you should be able to answer yes to each of these:

Following its short-lived Galaxy Z TriFold, Samsung appears to have a sequel on the way that’s set to arrive in the Galaxy Z Fold 9 lineup.

The Galaxy Z TriFold launched a few months after the Galaxy Z Fold 7, carrying the codename “Q7m.” GalaxyClub now reports that “Q9m” has surfaced, implying that Galaxy Z TriFold 2 will be based on the Galaxy Z Fold 9 series.

#10143. Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver

I help lead Google's agent skills program, currently with 175 agent skills that supplement community collections like go-skills. To keep that many skill files consistent, I wrote skill-lint, a standalone Go CLI that checks SKILL.md files and applies LLM-generated line edits before they ship. Even with skill-lint's own unit and fuzz test suite, a small slice or line-number mistake inside its Markdown parsers or edit applier can sit dormant until an unusual file or edit range triggers a runtime panic in the linter.

In Go, every slice or index operation that can panic at runtime compiles down to an explicit bounds-check trap in machine code, after the compiler's optimizer strips out the checks it can already rule out. To hunt for crashes, I compiled key functions from my code to see which panic traps survived optimization, and Gemini 4 Argon translated the path to each trap into rules for the Z3 constraint solver. An LLM-written solver model isn't a sound proof system, but it gives the agent an independent way to reason about control flow and synthesize concrete Go reproducers, and every crash it finds is real because go test runs the offending bytes directly. That workflow caught all three bugs I planted in test parsers and turned up three latent bugs in skill-lint.

In this post, I'll walk through how the Gemini and Z3 pipeline works, why go test -fuzz missed two of those crashes (and the one-line change that fixes it), and where this approach fits in a day-to-day Go workflow.

A recent post from Anthropic showed how formal verification catches latent bugs in C and C++ by having frontier AI models write machine-checked Rocq proofs across OSS-Fuzz libraries. Instead of sampling random inputs like a fuzzer, a formal tool works backward from each failure condition to solve for the exact input that triggers it. Full theorem proving is still too heavy for most day-to-day Go projects, so I wanted to see how much of that bug-hunting power an agent can get from an LLM and a constraint solver in about a minute per function.

In C and C++, reading or writing past the end of a buffer corrupts memory. Go catches out-of-bounds access at runtime instead, compiling every slice or index operation it can't prove safe into an explicit branch to runtime.panicBounds that panics, crashing the process unless recovered.

Before generating machine code, Go's SSA prove pass already eliminates most of those checks by tracking slice lengths and loop variables. That optimization pass leaves behind only the runtime.panicBounds traps the compiler couldn't rule out on its own, giving the solver a short list of candidate crash sites to target.

I compiled each target with GOOS=linux GOARCH=riscv64 go build -gcflags="-S -d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1" (-S prints the assembly listing and ssa/check_bce/debug=1 logs every surviving bounds check) and passed both the Go source and the disassembly to the model. Looking at Go source alone, you can't see which bounds checks the compiler already removed or where a register gets truncated to 8 bits; in the disassembly, both show up. I targeted RISC-V because it's the instruction set Anthropic's post targets for its Rocq proofs, and Go cross-compiles to it out of the box.

From there, Argon read the Go source and disassembly and returned a Z3 script modeling the path to each surviving trap, along with a patched function whenever it flagged a bug. Z3 then checked whether those constraints could be satisfied, and whenever it found a crashing input, go test replayed those bytes against the real function. Using an LLM saved me from translating assembly into solver constraints by hand. Argon's translation dominated the runtime, at about a minute per function, while Z3 itself finished in milliseconds.

Anthropic's approach relies on interactive theorem proving, where experts model machine semantics and Rocq checks LLM-generated proofs against those rules. In contrast, my workflow uses a constraint solver based on satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), relying on Argon to translate assembly directly into Z3 constraints. While a constraint solver doesn't provide a complete correctness proof without a semantic model, it is highly effective for finding bugs. Z3's check-sat command returns sat when input constraints can be satisfied and unsat when they cannot.

A sat answer ("definitely buggy") comes with concrete bytes aimed at the trap, and go test runs them against the real function. Once go test panics, you have a concrete bug reproducer regardless of whether Argon's model was sound. Like a Bloom filter for bugs, an unsat answer only means "maybe correct." Trading away a correctness proof is what makes the approach so practical: you get most of the bug-finding value of formal methods for a tiny fraction of the effort.

Anthropic's setup proved no-crash properties on whole binaries under a 64 MB budget; I checked individual functions on fresh 64-byte slices where cap(buf) == len(buf), so any slice past len(buf) panics. (If you want the full-binary Rocq setup for Go, theorem-labs/oss-verify includes a Go 1.27 runtime overlay that makes the runtime single-threaded and deterministic.)

For the fuzzing baseline, I ran unseeded go test -fuzz on Go 1.27.3 against each planted bug: one 3-second run and three 60-second runs, each with a fresh fuzz cache so a short time budget wouldn't explain a miss.

I started with three safe parsers to make sure the pipeline didn't flag clean code. The compiler's prove pass removed every bounds check in a TOML key parser on its own, and Z3 returned unsat on the remaining traps in an HTTP header scanner and a varint decoder.

Then I wrote three parsers with subtle panics. Here's the first one, ParseTwoChunkFrame:

In the RISC-V disassembly, the bug is much easier to see:

total := hdrLen + bodyLen adds two uint8 values, so MOVBU wraps the sum at 256 before the length guard checks it, while endBody adds the full 64-bit ints. Argon turned those instructions into a Z3 query asking whether a fresh slice of up to 64 bytes can pass the guard and still fail the endBody check at 0x0092:

Z3 returned a 59-byte counterexample with hdrLen = 48 and bodyLen = 236: their uint8 sum wraps from 284 down to 28 (so 28 + 4 ≤ 59 passes the guard), and buf[endHdr:endBody] then slices to index 288 and panics.

At 59 bytes, 19.4% of all possible (hdrLen, bodyLen) pairs trigger this crash. Yet a 3-second fuzz run missed it, and so did three 60-second runs.

Go checks a slice expression like buf[endHdr:endBody] against the slice's capacity, not its length, and Go's fuzzer rarely passes a slice without spare capacity. In a 10-second probe of 386,741 fuzz calls, 89% of inputs were views into a shared ~100 MB buffer, and only 0.07% had cap == len. With that much spare capacity, endBody (at most 514) never exceeds cap(buf), so the buggy parser returns bytes past the end of buf instead of panicking.

The second target, ExtractQuotedToken, hit the same blind spot when a trailing backslash pushed the index one byte past len(buf). Z3 caught it immediately with the 2-byte input []byte{'"', '\\'}, while the fuzzer absorbed the overrun in spare capacity.

Clipping capacity to length with a full slice expression turns any slice past len into a panic:

After that change, the fuzzer crashed both ParseTwoChunkFrame and ExtractQuotedToken in all three runs (median 0.28 s and 0.17 s). The third target, ParseMagicPacket, was a control because its signed int8 length bug panics on a negative index regardless of capacity, and the fuzzer found it in every run either way. Fuzzing still can't give you an unsat signal across the remaining paths, which is how I checked the three safe parsers and Argon's patches.

Next, I pointed the pipeline at skill-lint itself. A whole Go CLI is too large to hand to a solver directly. Even a 10-line parser links 1,559 symbols from the Go runtime, and the 28 MB skill-lint binary has 32,321 symbols in total. Following Functional Core, Imperative Shell, I left CLI flags, network calls, and file I/O to go test -fuzz and go test -race, and ran the solver only on pure functions and slice helpers extracted from file-reading code.

Of the five functions I tested, two scanners came back unsat (including a CRLF line splitter with six surviving bounds checks), and the other three had bugs. The sharpest was in ApplyReplacementChunks, which validates LLM-generated {StartLine, EndLine} edits against the initial line count and sorts them bottom-to-top so earlier edits don't shift later line numbers:

Z3 immediately returned sat because sorting by StartLine doesn't prevent two chunks from overlapping. In the extracted helper, which checks bounds once up front, replacing lines 3 and 4 of a 4-line file with one line shrinks lines to 3 elements, so a second chunk spanning lines 2 through 4 evaluates lines[4:] and panics with slice bounds out of range [4:3]. In the shipped ApplyChunks, a per-iteration bounds check turns that case into a misleading range error, while overlapping chunks that stay within len(lines) silently overwrite the earlier edit. Rejecting overlapping chunks after the sort fixes both.

The other two bugs were similar accounting errors. In the local fixer, target line numbers were checked once per violation before the inner chunk loop applied deletions that shrank the slice (a latent panic if a fixer ever returns a second chunk after a deletion, though DeleteLineFix only returns one today). In the prompt packer, a truncation check reserved a flat 100 bytes for a ~70-byte wrapper plus file path, overshooting the 2 MB context budget in the shipped code when a path exceeds about 30 bytes and panicking in the extracted helper.

When you check a function modularly like this, the target has to include its own entry-point guards (like the bounds check and sort in ApplyReplacementChunks). If an internal helper assumes preconditions that are only enforced by its caller or stated in a doc comment, Z3 will happily invent inputs that violate them. Because each extracted helper included its entry guards, false positives weren't an issue: across all six buggy functions in my tests, the first sat assignment Z3 returned triggered a real panic in go test without needing to filter out non-crashing candidates or loop back into the solver.

Once I pulled these helpers away from file I/O, a 3-second fuzz run caught all three bugs too. To make sure Argon wasn't leaning on source comments in my test files, I also reran the skill-lint targets with all comments stripped; Argon and Z3 still caught all three bugs and returned unsat on the two scanners and all three patches.

Staying entirely inside the target language makes a whole class of bugs hard for an agent to see. When an LLM reviews Go source directly, a line like if int(total)+4 > len(buf) looks like a textbook bounds check, and when it runs go test -fuzz, target-language runtime details like spare slice capacity or multi-step precondition checks can hide the crash indefinitely. Asking the agent to translate Go and assembly into a constraint solver forces a change of representation that strips away surface syntax and makes every bit width and slice bound explicit, while go test turns any solver hit back into a concrete Go reproducer.

For most Go code, fuzzing pure helpers with slice capacity clipped to length will catch bounds bugs in seconds. A solver is worth the extra minute on the traps that survive both the compiler's range prover and a quick fuzz run, especially in parsers and editors that compute offsets from multi-field headers or line ranges.

Single-threaded solver models don't see data races or deadlocks, so concurrent code still belongs with the race detector, deterministic concurrency testing, and Go 1.27's goroutine leak profiles.

If you're experimenting with solvers or coding agents on Go, let's compare notes on X or LinkedIn.

#10142. Granite Embedding Multilingual R2: Open Apache 2.0 Multilingual Embeddings with 32K Context — Best Sub-100M Retrieval Quality

TL;DR: Two new Apache 2.0 multilingual embedding models built on ModernBERT — a 97M-parameter compact model that beats every open sub-100M multilingual embedder on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (60.3), and a 311M full-size model that scores 65.2 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval (#2 among open models under 500M parameters) with Matryoshka support. Both cover 200+ languages, are tuned on 52 languages, handle 32K-token context (64x R1), and add code retrieval across 9 programming languages.

In this post: Enterprise-Ready by Design · A Strong Sub-100M Multilingual Model · What Changed from R1 · Training the Full-Size 311M Model · Building the compact 97M Multilingual Model · Benchmark Results · Matryoshka Embeddings · Deployment Options · For Framework Integrators · Which Model Should You Use? · Try The Models

Multilingual embedding models face a persistent tension: broad language coverage usually comes at the cost of model size, and small models usually sacrifice languages. If you work across languages — retrieval-augmented generation over multilingual corpora, cross-lingual search, code retrieval in international teams — you've likely had to choose between a model that's fast enough and one that's good enough.

The Granite Embedding Multilingual R2 release narrows that gap considerably. We're releasing two new multilingual embedding models:

Both models support 200+ languages with enhanced retrieval quality for 52 languages and programming code, handle context lengths up to 32,768 tokens (a 64x increase over their R1 predecessors), and are released under the Apache 2.0 license. They work out of the box with sentence-transformers and transformers, require no task-specific instructions, and are compatible as drop-in replacements in LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and Milvus with a one-line model name change. For frameworks currently using an English-only default, that one line gives every user in your community support for 200+ languages — no API changes, no new dependencies, no code changes required on their end. Both models ship with ONNX and OpenVINO weights for CPU-optimized inference.

The underlying encoder was pretrained on text from 200+ languages, producing general-purpose embeddings for any of them. The following 52 languages receive explicit retrieval-pair and cross-lingual training for higher-quality retrieval:

Albanian (sq), Arabic (ar), Azerbaijani (az), Bengali (bn), Bulgarian (bg), Catalan (ca), Chinese (zh), Croatian (hr), Czech (cs), Danish (da), Dutch (nl), English (en), Estonian (et), Finnish (fi), French (fr), Georgian (ka), German (de), Greek (el), Hebrew (he), Hindi (hi), Hungarian (hu), Icelandic (is), Indonesian (id), Italian (it), Japanese (ja), Kazakh (kk), Khmer (km), Korean (ko), Latvian (lv), Lithuanian (lt), Malay (ms), Marathi (mr), Norwegian (no), Persian (fa), Polish (pl), Portuguese (pt), Romanian (ro), Russian (ru), Serbian (sr), Slovak (sk), Slovenian (sl), Spanish (es), Swahili (sw), Swedish (sv), Tagalog (tl), Telugu (te), Thai (th), Turkish (tr), Ukrainian (uk), Urdu (ur), Uzbek (uz), Vietnamese (vi).

Additionally, the models are trained on programming code (Python, Go, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, SQL, C, C++) and support cross-lingual code retrieval.

Both embedding models are trained on a mixture of IBM‑curated datasets, publicly available data, and internally generated or synthetic data. Public web‑derived data used in training is selected and filtered using IBM‑developed quality, deduplication, and governance processes intended to reduce risk in downstream commercial use. We intentionally avoid the use of the MS‑MARCO training dataset and datasets with explicit non‑commercial licensing restrictions. The models are pretrained using GneissWeb, an IBM‑curated dataset derived from publicly available web content and processed using IBM’s data preparation and governance tooling—along with additional IBM‑curated and other publicly available sources. Datasets undergo IBM governance review to assess licensing considerations, ownership signals, and personal data risks. These processes are designed to contribute to responsible use and enterprise deployment.

The standout of this release is granite-embedding-97m-multilingual-r2. At 97 million parameters, it scores 60.3 on Multilingual MTEB Retrieval across 18 languages — the highest retrieval score we've found for any open multilingual embedding model under 100M parameters. The next-best model in that size class, multilingual-e5-small, scores 50.9 on the same benchmark — a +9.4 point gap on a mature benchmark.

At roughly one-third the size of the 311M full-size model, it retains the majority of its retrieval quality across multilingual, code, and long-document benchmarks — a +12.2 point gain on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval over its direct predecessor, driven by a new architecture, better training data, and a novel pruning methodology (more on that below). The full-size granite-embedding-311m-multilingual-r2 scores 65.2 on the same benchmark, a +13.0 point gain over its R1 predecessor.

The Granite Embedding Multilingual R1 models were built on XLM-RoBERTa encoders with a 512-token context window. The R2 generation is a ground-up rebuild:

ModernBERT is a recent encoder architecture that revisits the original BERT design with techniques from the last five years of transformer research. The shift brings several practical benefits: alternating attention lengths reduce computation on long sequences (improves throughput on long sequences significantly), rotary position embeddings allow the 32K context window without the positional interpolation hacks that plague older architectures, and Flash Attention 2.0 support speeds up encoding on modern GPUs.

The new multilingual tokenizers are worth highlighting. Rather than reusing XLM-RoBERTa's 250K-token vocabulary, we adopted existing tokenizers with strong multilingual and code coverage. The 311M model uses the Gemma 3 tokenizer (262K tokens); the 97M model starts from the GPT-OSS tokenizer and prunes it down to a compact 180K-token vocabulary that preserves broad multilingual coverage while reducing the embedding table's parameter footprint. Tokenizer efficiency matters more than people realize — a 32K-token window sounds impressive until your tokenizer burns half of it encoding a single paragraph of Thai.

The 311M model is a 22-layer ModernBERT encoder with a 262K-token multilingual vocabulary, trained through a multi-stage pipeline:

The result is a model that scores 65.2 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval and 56.3 on the overall average — a +14.5 point average gain over its R1 predecessor.

The 97M model is trained through a combination of vocabulary selection and knowledge distillation:

This approach transfers retrieval-specific knowledge from multiple strong teachers, while reducing the model parameters without sacrificing language coverage. The result is a highly efficient compact model — scoring 60.3 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval vs. 65.2 for the full-size model, while being approximately 3x smaller.

Performance across the main benchmark suite sorted by model size. Scores are averages across tasks within each benchmark (higher is better):

Encoding speed matters for production workloads, especially when you're indexing millions of documents or need low-latency query encoding. We measured latency and throughput on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU using 512-token chunks:

The 97M model encodes over 2,500 documents per second — comparable throughput to multilingual-e5-small — while delivering substantially higher retrieval quality. The 311M model, at ~1,800 docs/sec, performs better than jina-embeddings-v5-text-nano on retrieval quality (65.2 vs. 63.3) at over 5.5x the encoding speed (note: speed numbers are computed with the latest transformer code, which had a speed regression vs the last 4.57 version - for both the Jina and granite models - see our technical report for details). harrier-oss-v1-270m offers the best combination of speed and retrieval score among the competitors listed here.

The 311M model supports Matryoshka Representation Learning, which lets you truncate embeddings from the full 768 dimensions down to 512, 384, 256, or 128 with graceful quality degradation. This is useful when storage, memory, or similarity-computation cost is a concern — a 256-dimensional embedding takes one-third the storage of a 768-dimensional one, and cosine similarity is proportionally cheaper to compute.

Here's how retrieval quality holds up across embedding dimensions:

The quality loss from dimension reduction is remarkably small. Cutting from 768 to 256 dimensions — a 3x reduction in storage and similarity-computation cost — drops MTEB Multilingual Retrieval by just 0.5 points (65.2 → 64.7) and Code Retrieval by 0.5 points (63.9 → 63.4). Even at 128 dimensions (a 6x reduction), the model still scores 63.7 on MTEB Multilingual Retrieval and 62.3 on Code — retaining over 97% of its full-dimension performance. In practice, this means you can substantially reduce your index size and search latency with minimal impact on result quality. (Note,results in the above picture were evaluated with a context length of 1024 for English and Multilingual Retrieval, and 8192 for Code).

For comparison, the 311M model truncated to 384 dimensions (the same dimensionality as the 97M model's native output) still outperforms the 97M model across all three benchmarks. If you need 384-dimensional embeddings and can afford the 311M model's encoding cost, Matryoshka truncation is the stronger option.

The 97M model does not support Matryoshka — 384 dimensions is already compact.

Average performance on cross-lingual tasks within MTEB Retrieval. Belebele measures cross-lingual passage matching across 122 languages; MLQA measures extractive cross-lingual question answering retrieval across 7 languages.

The 311M R2 model gains +4.3 on Belebele and +4.1 on MLQA over its R1 predecessor, showing improved cross-lingual transfer at the larger scale across both benchmarks.

The 97M R2 model scores lower on Belebele (52.9 vs 55.1, −2.2) while matching its R1 predecessor on MLQA (60.5). The Belebele gap is a tradeoff inherent in the pruning and vocabulary reduction process — the R2 model's training prioritized the broader 18-language MTEB Multilingual Retrieval set (where it gains +12.2 over R1) and long-document retrieval (+31.3), while the smaller vocabulary (180K vs. 250K tokens) and reduced layer count (12 vs. 22) affect narrow cross-lingual transfer tasks. If cross-lingual transfer across many language pairs is your primary use case, the full-size 311M model is the better choice.

Both models ship with multiple deployment paths for production use. Install the core library with:

Sentence Transformers (recommended for most users):

LangChain (pip install langchain-huggingface):

LlamaIndex (pip install llama-index-embeddings-huggingface):

Both models also ship with pre-converted ONNX and OpenVINO weights for optimized CPU/accelerator inference, work as embedding endpoints via vLLM (vllm serve ... --task embed), and can be converted to GGUF for Ollama using llama.cpp. See the model cards for full deployment examples.

If you maintain an embedding framework, vector store, or RAG pipeline library and are evaluating these models as a default, here's what you need to know:

To discuss adopting these models as a default in your project, open an issue at ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models.

These two multilingual models are part of the broader Granite Embedding R2 family, which also includes two high-performing English-focused models: granite-embedding-english-r2 (149M parameters) and granite-embedding-small-english-r2 (47M parameters). If your data is predominantly English, the English models offer higher retrieval quality on English benchmarks at a smaller footprint, since they don't need to allocate capacity across 200+ languages.

Both models are available now on Hugging Face under the IBM Granite Embedding collection:

You can try the small models interactively (on CPU) via a Granite Embedding demo here on Hugging Face Spaces, or run the full examples notebook in Google Colab:

You can access our detailed technical report covering the full training methodology, per-language evaluations, and pruning ablations here Granite Multilingual Embedding R2 report. For questions, feedback, or issues, visit ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models on GitHub.

Framework maintainers: If you'd like to adopt these models as a default in your project, open an issue at ibm-granite/granite-embedding-models — we're happy to help with integration, testing, and any questions about licensing or deployment.

Give them a try, and if the embeddings spark joy, smash that ❤️ button on Hugging Face. Our models have feelings too, and every +1 keeps them warm at night.

#10140. PaddleOCR 3.5: Running OCR and Document Parsing Tasks with a Transformers Backend

PaddleOCR 3.5 brings OCR and document parsing tasks closer to the Hugging Face ecosystem. With this release, supported PaddleOCR models can run with Hugging Face Transformers as an inference backend by setting:

PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR model series such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing model series such as PaddleOCR-VL 1.5, while Transformers becomes one of the supported backends for running them.

Try the live demo on Hugging Face Spaces: https://huggingface.co/spaces/PaddlePaddle/paddleocr-3.5-transformers-demo

PaddleOCR 3.5 introduces a more flexible inference-engine interface. Developers can select the backend through the engine parameter and pass backend-specific options through engine_config.

This release is mainly about the inference backend layer: PaddleOCR continues to provide OCR and document parsing capabilities, while Transformers gives supported PaddleOCR models another backend option that fits naturally into Hugging Face-centered environments. The larger Document AI workflow remains in the hands of developers and application builders.

For RAG, Document AI, and document agent applications, the hard part often starts before the LLM.

Developers first need to turn PDFs, scanned documents, screenshots, tables, charts, formulas, and complex page layouts into reliable structured data. If this ingestion step is weak, the downstream LLM workflow may miss key information, retrieve the wrong context, or produce unreliable answers.

PaddleOCR helps address this document ingestion challenge by providing OCR series models such as PP-OCRv5 and document parsing series models such as PaddleOCR-VL-1.5.

With PaddleOCR 3.5, these capabilities are now easier to connect with Transformers-centered stacks. Supported PaddleOCR models can run with a Transformers backend, while PaddleOCR continues to manage the OCR or document parsing pipeline behind the scenes.

For developers, this means less integration friction and a more natural path from documents to downstream RAG, agent, search, analytics, or automation workflows.

Install PaddleOCR 3.5, PaddleX, Transformers, and a compatible PyTorch build for your hardware.

For CPU, ROCm, or other environments, install the PyTorch build that matches your target hardware.

The Hugging Face Space uses float32 for broad compatibility. For your own hardware, you can tune backend-specific options through engine_config:

The best configuration depends on your model, hardware, and deployment environment.

Use the Transformers backend when you want PaddleOCR’s OCR and document parsing capabilities to fit more naturally into a Hugging Face-centered stack.

This is especially useful if you are building RAG, Document AI, search, analytics, or agent applications and already rely on PyTorch / Transformers infrastructure for model loading, experimentation, deployment, or model artifact management.

The Transformers backend is a good fit when you want:

When maximizing OCR or document parsing throughput is the priority, PaddleOCR’s default paddle_static backend is usually the recommended choice.

This release is not about replacing one backend with another. It is about giving developers more flexibility: use PaddleOCR for OCR and document parsing capabilities, and choose the inference backend that best fits your stack.

Try the PaddleOCR 3.5 Transformers demo on Hugging Face Spaces:

https://huggingface.co/spaces/PaddlePaddle/paddleocr-3.5-transformers-demo

https://huggingface.co/PaddlePaddle/models

PaddleOCR 3.5 brings OCR and document parsing capabilities closer to Transformers-centered workflows, while giving developers the freedom to build the larger Document AI applications around them.

Special thanks to Anton Vlasjuk for his end-to-end involvement, including reviewing and merging all related pull requests.

We also appreciate Raushan Turganbay and Yoni Gozlan for their valuable PR reviews and feedback.

#10139. How to Add AI Facial Expression Editing to Your Video Pipeline (2026)

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Product teams keep asking engineers for the same feature: “Can users fix the reaction in this clip without reshooting it?” It lands on the backlog as “add expression editing,” and it hides a lot of decisions.

This guide compares the realistic integration options in 2026, sketches a pipeline architecture, models costs, includes a small runnable job helper, and covers the consent and audit logging you need before changing a real person’s face. Vendor details change quickly, so check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Information about features, pricing, APIs and policies in this article was checked on November 10, 2026 and may change. Check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Performance transfer is great for animation, but someone has to record a new take for every change. If your promise is “fix the reaction in the footage you already have,” direct editing fits better.

DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

For developers, SyncMonster publishes public API documentation for DRAMA. Here is what those docs state, as checked on November 10, 2026:

A few things to note honestly. The same generate endpoint also serves other SyncMonster features behind their own flags, so read the parameter table carefully. In the version we checked, the parameter table marks an audio input as required on generate, and the drama-only example includes one, so plan for that in your request builder. The emotion values exposed in the API are the four core emotions, and the extra app presets did not appear in the API docs. The docs describe polling only, with no webhooks mentioned, and they do not publish rate limits, an SDK, or a numeric maximum video duration (an error code exists for exceeding a duration limit).

Runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

Runway’s API pricing guide lists Act-Two at 5 credits per second of output, with credits priced at $0.01 each, so $0.05 per second. Earlier documentation mentioned a 15-credit minimum per generation, and the current pricing page does not list one, so check for minimums before you budget short clips. The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

The catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the new reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

LivePortrait is an open-source portrait animation framework from Kuaishou’s KwaiVGI group. It animates a source image or video using a driving video or a saved motion template, supports video-to-video portrait editing, and offers retargeting controls for eyes and lips.

The README sets up a Python 3.10 conda environment and expects Git and FFmpeg, with an NVIDIA GPU recommended. It also notes that Apple Silicon runs roughly 20x slower than an RTX 4090, and that Humans mode needs PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 on a Mac. That matters if you were hoping to prototype on a MacBook and ship the same setup. A basic run adapted from the README looks like this:

Here -s is the source portrait (an image or video) and -d is the driving clip. Retargeting is exposed through additional options and the Gradio interface, so check the README for current names because they change between releases. Also read the repository’s license file before you plan any commercial use.

The Hugging Face Spaces demo is handy for experiments, but production means owning GPU provisioning, queueing, model updates and quality review. You still steer with a driving input rather than a “happier by 30%” control.

Rule of thumb: if expression editing is a feature rather than your product, buy. If you need on-prem processing or model-level changes, build on LivePortrait and budget for ops.

Whatever the backend, the pipeline has five stages.

Here is the shape of the worker loop. This is illustrative pseudocode only, not any vendor’s SDK or real endpoints:

The idempotency and backoff tips below are easy to get wrong, so here is a small vendor-neutral module. The key function hashes the input file together with the parameters, so a retry with the same input maps to the same job. The poller backs off exponentially up to a ceiling and gives up after a maximum wait. It uses only the Python standard library.

A short test confirms the behavior: the same input gives the same key regardless of parameter order, different parameters give a different key, and the poller returns once the state becomes done.

Credits are not a shared currency across vendors, so compare units first and money second.

For prototyping, the DRAMA web app has a free plan (60 credits, 1080p, up to 2 minutes of processing, 2 projects, watermarked output), which is enough to judge quality on your own sample footage before writing integration code. The docs we checked list API billing in credits but do not state a dollar price per API credit, so confirm that with SyncMonster before you finalize a pricing model. Do not assume web-app plan credits convert at the same rate as API credits.

Plan details are as listed by the vendor on November 10, 2026 and can change.

Changing a real person’s expression can change what viewers believe they felt, so treat this as a product requirement.

For a product feature that edits reactions in existing footage, the DRAMA API is the most direct hosted option among those compared here: face detection with thumbnails for selection, per-face edits, and emotion values you set in code, with no driving performance. Go in knowing its current limits: four emotion parameters in the API, polling instead of webhooks, and no published rate limits or SDK. Starting with the free plan on your own clips is a low-risk way to judge quality. Product details and API access for this AI expression changer are on SyncMonster’s site.

Choose the Runway API if your users want to animate characters from an acted performance. Choose LivePortrait if you need on-prem processing or model-level control and have the GPU and ops capacity. Leave Flawless DeepEditor to studio editorial teams, and Photoshop to still-image workflows.

Yes. DRAMA by SyncMonster has a hosted REST API for editing expressions in existing video using emotion values, and Runway offers Act-Two through its API for performance transfer. LivePortrait is open source and can be wrapped in your own service.

Yes, with a direct editing tool. The DRAMA API takes emotion values from 0 to 1 for happy, sad, excited and angry on a selected face. Runway Act-Two and LivePortrait both expect a driving performance or motion template.

Run face detection first, let the user pick a face, then send that face’s ID with the edit request. The DRAMA API returns a face ID and a thumbnail for each detected face for this purpose.

Per vendor docs as of November 10, 2026: the DRAMA API bills 0.5 credit per second for face detection and 1 credit per second for drama generation, while Runway’s Act-Two API bills 5 credits per second at $0.01 per credit. LivePortrait costs whatever your GPU time costs.

Yes, but its README notes Apple Silicon can be about 20x slower than an RTX 4090. An NVIDIA GPU is recommended for anything beyond experiments.

Not a public one. DeepEditor is an Avid Media Composer extension with access by application, aimed at film and TV editorial teams.

Log the requester, consent record, selected face, emotion and intensity, backend used, input and output hashes, credits used, and a timestamp, and keep the original file.

#10137. Introducing the Ettin Reranker Family

Today I'm releasing six new Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder rerankers, state-of-the-art at their respective sizes, built on top of the Ettin ModernBERT encoders, together with the data and full training recipe that produced them:

The models were trained with a distillation recipe: pointwise MSE on mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 scores over cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, which is a subset of lightonai/embeddings-pre-training mixed with a reranked subset of lightonai/embeddings-fine-tuning.

Our six rerankers paired with google/embeddinggemma-300m on MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval. See Results for five more embedder pairings.

If you're new to rerankers and want the "why" first, jump to What is a reranker, and why pair one with an embedder?. If you just want to plug a model in, jump to Usage. If you want to train your own, jump to Training.

I bootstrapped the training recipe below with the new train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. Install it with hf skills add train-sentence-transformers [--global] [--claude] and ask your AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...) to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data.

A reranker (a.k.a. pointwise cross-encoder) is a neural model that takes a (query, document) pair and outputs a single relevance score. Unlike an embedding model, which encodes the query and document separately and computes their similarity from the two embedding vectors, a reranker lets the two texts attend to each other through every transformer layer. That joint encoding is more accurate but also more expensive: the model has to be run once per (query, document) pair rather than once per text.

Because cross-encoders are too expensive to run over a full corpus, the common production pattern is retrieve-then-rerank: a fast embedding model retrieves the top-K candidates (cheap), then a cross-encoder re-orders just those K with high accuracy. The total cost stays bounded while the final ranking is much closer to what an exhaustive cross-encoder pass would produce.

Throughout this blogpost I'll use "reranker" and "cross-encoder" interchangeably.

The released models are normal Sentence Transformers CrossEncoder models, so you can use them with just 3 lines of code:

For a query and a list of candidates, you can also use rank to get back sorted indices and scores:

You can swap cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-32m-v1 for any other size to trade quality for speed. All six accept up to 8K tokens of context (useful for long-document reranking) thanks to ModernBERT's long-context pre-training.

It is recommended to install kernels and set model_kwargs={"dtype": "bfloat16", "attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"} for the highest throughput. See the Speed section below for more details, but in general you can expect a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over default loading depending on model size and sequence length.

A complete example with a fast embedder for retrieval and the reranker for the final ordering:

This is the same shape used by most modern search systems. The retriever decides what enters the funnel, the reranker decides what wins.

All six rerankers share the same architecture and differ only in their backbone size. The backbone is one of the six Ettin encoders from Johns Hopkins University's Ettin suite. These are ModernBERT-style models with unpadded attention, RoPE positional encodings, GeGLU, and 2T tokens of open-license pre-training, supporting up to 8192 tokens of context.

On top of each encoder, the reranker uses a 4-module classification head that mirrors ModernBertForSequenceClassification but is built from Sentence Transformers' modular components. The underlying Transformer is a plain AutoModel rather than AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which lets us use sequence unpadding for variable-length inputs for Flash Attention 2. At medium-document sequence lengths this is a 1.7x-8.3x speedup over fp32+SDPA depending on model size (see Speed for the full benchmark):

In my ablations, CLS pooling outperformed mean pooling. That was a little surprising. ModernBERT uses global attention only every third layer and the other two-thirds use local-window attention that cannot reach CLS from distant positions. Empirically, those few global layers carry enough signal to make CLS the better pooling choice.

All six models are released under the Apache 2.0 license, matching the Ettin encoders.

I ran each released model through the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark (10 tasks, top-100 reranked) using MTEB's two-stage reranking flow, pairing each reranker with six embedding models that span the speed/quality spectrum:

The dashed retriever-only line in each chart below is the headline number to beat. Anything below it means the reranker actively hurts the pipeline on average:

Mean NDCG@10 over the 6 embedder pairings, sorted descending. Our six models are in bold, and the teacher mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2 is underlined.

† Capped to max_seq_length=8192 (the 4B Qwen3-based rerankers don't fit on a single H100 80GB at native context). Native-context evaluation is likely higher.

NanoBEIR is a fast 13-dataset subset of BEIR that uses 50 queries per dataset against up to 5000 documents each. NanoBEIR is what metric_for_best_model was set to during training (see Evaluation), and what I used to guide the experimentation.

The smallest model I'm releasing, our 17M, beats the 33M ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2 by +0.051 NDCG@10 (0.5576 vs 0.5066) on MTEB and +0.038 (0.6746 vs 0.6369) on NanoBEIR at roughly half the parameter count. The 32M beats the 568M BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 by +0.025 (0.5779 vs 0.5526) on MTEB, a 17x parameter gap. If you've been using one of the legacy MiniLM rerankers as the default in your retrieve-then-rerank stack, swapping in our 17M (or 32M) is a low-risk drop-in replacement, with a noticeable quality bump on both benchmarks.

Moving up the table, our 150M is the strongest reranker I tested in the under-600M range on MTEB, edging out the recent Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (596M) by +0.005 (0.5994 vs 0.5940) and beating every BAAI bge-reranker variant by 0.03 to 0.05. The 68M is also worth a mention: at 0.5915 it lands almost exactly on Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B (0.5940) while using a ninth of the parameters.

At the top of the released range, our 1B model closely tracks its teacher. It comes within 0.0001 of the 1.54B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 on MTEB (0.6114 vs 0.6115) and within 0.008 on NanoBEIR, despite distilling from a model 54% larger than itself. The distillation effectively closes the gap to the teacher, which is what I was hoping to see going into this release.

The overall strongest reranker in the comparison is Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-4B at 0.6367 MTEB, +0.025 above our 1B model. Closing that gap from the current recipe would likely require distilling from a stronger teacher (our teacher itself sits below Qwen3-Reranker-4B). For most retrieve-then-rerank workloads, our 1B at a quarter of the parameters (see Speed) is a much more practical pick.

Quality numbers are only half of what matters for a reranker. The other half is whether its latency fits inside the budget you have between retrieval and showing results to the user. Let me walk through what I measured.

I benchmarked all six released models against thirteen public rerankers (strong baselines up to about 1B parameters) on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB. The queries and documents come from sentence-transformers/natural-questions at its natural document-length distribution: most NQ answers are short, some are long. Documents are truncated at max_length=512 to avoid giving the older models an unfair advantage. Each model uses its best supported attention implementation: Flash Attention 2 wherever the architecture supports it (BERT, XLM-RoBERTa, ModernBERT, Qwen2), SDPA where it doesn't, and eager for DeBERTa-v2 (which currently has neither FA2 nor SDPA support in transformers).

For every model an auto-batch search starts at batch size 8 and doubles until the GPU runs out of memory. At each batch size I run three timed passes and keep the median throughput, so a single unlucky run doesn't drag the number around. The reported throughput is at whichever batch size won.

Table 1. Throughput in pairs per second, all in bfloat16. Our six rerankers are in bold.

Our 17M is the fastest reranker in the whole comparison, at 7517 pairs per second. That's almost twice the throughput of ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (3817) and faster even than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (4029). And as you saw in the MTEB table earlier, our 17M is also more accurate than every MiniLM variant. If you're currently running a MiniLM cross-encoder, swapping to our 17M is a one-line change that improves both your latency and search quality.

Our 150M is an even more interesting comparison, because there are two direct architectural peers at exactly 150M parameters: Alibaba-NLP/gte-reranker-modernbert-base and ibm-granite/granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2. Both are built on the same ModernBERT-base backbone. Our 150M runs at 3237 pairs per second, while the two peers come in at 1418 and 1404 respectively, for a 2.3x speed gap.

All three 150M models use Flash Attention 2, but the two peers load through AutoModelForSequenceClassification, which keeps the inputs padded. So attention itself runs the FA2 kernel, but the rest of the model is still doing dense compute on padding tokens that don't contribute anything. Our modular Transformer module (see Architecture Details above) propagates unpadded inputs all the way through the model, so every layer only spends compute on real tokens. That's the difference between getting some of FA2's benefit and getting all of it.

At the bottom of the table, our 1B model hits 928 pairs per second, which is 2.4x faster than the 1.54B teacher mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (387 pairs per second) while matching its MTEB score within 0.0001. The teacher is Qwen2-based with a prompt-template overhead per pair, so the distilled student inherits the teacher's calibration and judgement but skips all the runtime baggage. This is honestly the most satisfying single number in the whole release for me.

One unfortunate note: the DeBERTa-v2-based mxbai-rerank-{xsmall,base,large}-v1 series ends up much slower than the rest of the table because DeBERTa-v2 currently supports neither Flash Attention 2 nor SDPA in transformers. The 70M mxbai-rerank-xsmall-v1 runs at 2636 pairs per second, about half the throughput of our 68M at almost the same parameter count. The models themselves are perfectly fine, they just don't get to use modern attention kernels.

If you're self-hosting on a consumer card rather than a datacenter GPU, here's the same throughput sweep on an RTX 3090. Same benchmark setup as Table 1: bfloat16, best-supported attention per model, three-trial median throughput at the largest batch that fits.

Our 17M is still the fastest model in the table at 9008 pairs per second, actually higher than its H100 number, which suggests that at tiny sizes raw compute isn't the bottleneck and the H100's extra muscle doesn't translate. The middle of the table reshuffles a bit, with the MiniLM rerankers overtaking our 32M and 68M, and the 1B slipping behind mxbai-rerank-base-v2 (189 vs 221 pairs per second). Our 150M model still holds a solid lead over the two 150M ModernBERT-based peers, and the teacher-replacement story still holds, with our 1B at 2.7x the throughput of the 1.5B mxbai-rerank-large-v2 (189 vs 69 pairs per second).

On CPU, we can't take advantage of bf16, Flash Attention 2, or unpadding, so the latency story is a bit simpler: the higher the parameter count, the slower the model. The 17M model is considerably faster than ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 (267.4 vs 143.9 pairs per second) and even faster than the smaller ms-marco-MiniLM-L4-v2 (206.2). As expected, our 150M model lands alongside the two 150M peers (14.0 vs 14.5 and 14.7 pairs per second) now that unpadding no longer applies. If you're CPU-bound, our 17M and 32M are the practical picks.

To explain where the speed comes from, the next table sweeps fp32+SDPA, bf16+SDPA, and bf16+FA2 for our six models using the same bench config. The FA2 column is split in two: one with the inputs still padded (what a wrapped model would see) and one with unpadded inputs (what our modular Transformer actually does). The rightmost column is what our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

Table 2. Precision and attention ablation for the six released sizes at max_length=512 on natural NQ documents. Each cell shows pairs / second with the multiplier relative to fp32+SDPA in parentheses, and peak GPU memory on the second line. The rightmost column (in bold) is the configuration our models use by default when FA2 is enabled.

The total speedup from bf16+FA2 w.o. padding over the fp32+SDPA baseline grows sharply with model size, from 1.71x on the 17M to 8.26x on the 1B. Most of that growth comes from bf16 alone: the fp32+SDPA to bf16+SDPA step gives the 17M only a 1.03x speedup but gives the 1B a full 5.60x speedup, also due to the lowered memory cost allowing for bigger batch sizes. In short, bfloat16 is the biggest single contributor to the overall speedup.

Unexpectedly, turning on FA2 while the inputs are still padded is actually slower than bf16+SDPA at every size in the release. The FA2 kernel prefers an unpadded format, and when you feed it padded inputs you pay the bookkeeping overhead of converting between formats while still spending compute on the padding tokens themselves. So the bf16+FA2 w. padding column is roughly what you'd measure if you swapped sdpa for flash_attention_2 in model_kwargs without changing anything else about the model loader. This is the situation that gte-reranker-modernbert-base and granite-embedding-reranker-english-r2 from Table 1 are in.

Lastly, going from bf16+FA2 w. padding to bf16+FA2 w.o. padding is worth between 1.78x (1B) and 2.45x (68M) of additional throughput, and it also cuts peak memory considerably, allowing for higher batch sizes.

So my recommendation is simple: enable bf16 and FA2 together. The six Ettin rerankers will use unpadded inputs by default, since that's what the modular Transformer module from the Architecture Details section is set up for. The full snippet is the same as in the Usage section above:

Use pip install kernels to install FA2. It ships pre-built kernels for a wide range of GPU architectures, CUDA versions, and operating systems.

One caveat for other CrossEncoders: the full speedup is only available for models built with a modular Transformer like the Ettin rerankers. Applying the same two flags to a CrossEncoder that loads through AutoModelForSequenceClassification lands you in the slower bf16+FA2 w. padding column of Table 2 instead.

The training script below started as the output of the new train-sentence-transformers Agent Skill, shipped in Sentence Transformers v5.5.0. If you use an AI coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, ...), you can install the skill and ask it to fine-tune a SentenceTransformer, CrossEncoder, or SparseEncoder model on your data. The skill carries version-aware guidance for base model selection, loss and evaluator choice, hard-negative mining, distillation, LoRA, Matryoshka, multilingual training, and static embeddings, plus template scripts for each model type.

A prompt like "Fine-tune a cross-encoder reranker on (query, document) pairs from my dataset, mine hard negatives, and push to my Hub repo" will produce a runnable script you can then iterate on. That's how I started working on the recipe below.

All six rerankers were trained with the same single-stage recipe. Only the learning rate and the per-device batch size vary per model size. The full training script is ~150 lines and uses one published dataset.

The recipe converged after a single sweep across model sizes. Each size's learning rate was tuned by a small grid search on a ~15% subset of the final training data, and the resulting LRs transferred cleanly to the full-data runs without re-tuning. No per-size tuning beyond LR was needed.

Most published reranker recipes train on human-labeled relevance triples (a query, one positive document, and optionally hard negatives) with a contrastive, pointwise, pairwise, or listwise loss like MultipleNegativesRankingLoss, BinaryCrossEntropyLoss, RankNetLoss, or LambdaLoss, respectively. See my earlier Training and Finetuning Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost, for example.

But this approach has a few practical and theoretical drawbacks. First, positives need to be human-labeled, which is expensive and slow to scale across many domains. Second, the model only ever sees a label for the small subset of (query, document) pairs that someone went through. Especially after hard negative mining, you end up with a lot of false negatives, e.g. as shown in Hard Negatives, Hard Lessons. Third, the binary nature of this labeling doesn't match reality, where some documents are simply more relevant than others.

I took a different route here: pointwise MSE distillation from an existing strong teacher reranker. The setup is simple enough to describe in three lines:

I've released the training data as a single Hugging Face dataset, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data, assembled from two sources. Each source is kept as its own split so the provenance is transparent:

Total: ~143M (query, document, score) triples, plus a held-out 5K-row eval split (the tail of quora) that drives the in-training eval loss.

Most hyperparameters are constant across model sizes:

Only the learning rate and global batch size very per model size.

global_batch_size is per_device_batch_size x world_size x gradient_accumulation_steps. On a single 8-GPU node, the 1024 global batch for 17m means per_device=128. On 8 nodes, it means per_device=8. The training script computes per_device_batch_size from global_batch_size // world_size so the same script works at any node count. The global batch size could be made more consistent, but I found that the above values worked well and didn't want to retune them just for the sake of consistency.

I monitored NanoBEIR mean NDCG@10 during training (eval every 5% of steps) and used it as the metric_for_best_model for load_best_model_at_end. NanoBEIR is fast, so I could afford it 20 times per training run. After training, I evaluated both the best checkpoint (according to NanoBEIR) and the last checkpoint on the full MTEB(eng, v2) Retrieval benchmark. The final release checkpoint was the one that did best on MTEB. The NanoBEIR-preferred checkpoint won for all sizes except 68m, where the last checkpoint was slightly stronger.

The complete script (what every released model was trained with) is a single file. Only ENCODER_SIZE changes per run, and everything else is automatic:

For multi-node training (anything past 17m/32m), launch the same script with torchrun:

The ettin-reranker-v1 family, trained with a single simple recipe, is state-of-the-art at every released size up to 1B parameters. Pointwise MSE distillation from a strong teacher onto a broad-domain and retrieval-specific mix scales cleanly from 17M to 1B parameters, with only the learning rate and per-device batch size changing between sizes.

Every ettin-reranker-v1 model beats the ms-marco-MiniLM-L*-v2 family by a comfortable margin on MTEB and NanoBEIR. cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-150m-v1 is the strongest mid-tier reranker I tested in the under-600M range, cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-400m-v1 lands within 0.0024 of the 1.54B teacher's MTEB score, and cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-1b-v1 matches that teacher within 0.0001.

If you build something on top of these, please let me know! I'd genuinely love to see what people do with them, and if you manage to train better rerankers using the released data, even better. The recipe is intentionally simple, partly so that there's plenty of headroom for someone else to improve it. Train a stronger teacher and the same script can keep producing better students.

I'd like to thank the Ettin team (Orion Weller, Kathryn Ricci, Marc Marone, Antoine Chaffin, Dawn Lawrie, and Benjamin Van Durme) for building the base encoders that these rerankers are built on, the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for their work on the training data collection, and the Mixedbread AI team (Xianming Li, Aamir Shakir, Rui Huang, Tsz-fung Andrew Lee, Julius Lipp, Benjamin Clavié, and Jing Li) for their work on the teacher model.

If you use the ettin-reranker-v1 family or any of the released artifacts, please cite this blogpost:

This is a fantastic read, thank you for the hard work and for sharing the recipes!

Great work! Really learnt a lot from this blog.

Great work! Love that you used stratified sampling.It's great to see its power on cross-encoders, too!

Definitely! I tried a few variants, and in my tests, a mix of top and stratified worked best, but I sampled from 2048 docs, so fully stratified means the 2nd doc is already pretty far from the most similar.

What a clean release, congrats @tomaarsen !

Thanks Maxime! You know, I bet the training script would apply pretty cleanly on LFM models as well 👀Although maybe the model prefers a generative architecture with a chat template that asks the model to generate either "yes" or "no", and the difference in raw logit scores for those tokens are used as the prediction. That's what's used for the teacher model's Sentence Transformers integration, and it works quite well: https://huggingface.co/mixedbread-ai/mxbai-rerank-large-v2

Fantastic work! In information retrieval, rerankers are often used in real-time pipelines, so a compact reranker with strong performance is exactly what many of us have been waiting for. Thank you for the great work!

Yess, exactly. In my opinion, rerankers have been getting too big to keep them usable. Hopefully this'll inspire others to make smaller models as well. Plus, the Ettin base models are just amazing, that helps a lot.

Since I often use TEI (text-embeddings-inference) in production, I opened a pull request adding Ettin support to TEI, though I’m not sure if it will be merged.

With this, Ettin can be served as a stable API service through TEI, and I observed around a 1.5x inference speedup in my tests!

Amazing work @tomaarsen , thanks for everything you do for open source !May I ask some questions on the recipe ?

If I understand well, you are mixing lightOn hard negatives data (with Jang et al. stratified sampling) with broader lightonai/embeddings-pre-training - which (i think) doesn't include mined negatives

Correct on all counts. They're different data formats initially. I took:

Yes, I did try various mixes. Specifically, I tried multiple approaches for the second subsampling (256 -> 64), e.g. grabbing 16 random docs, grabbing top 8 + 8 random, top 16 + 16 random, top 16 + 16 uniformly sampled, top 32, top 64, and what worked best for me: 32 top + 32 uniformly subsampled.

I also tried different mixes of the pre-training data vs the embeddings-fine-tuning data. As you can see https://huggingface.co/datasets/cross-encoder/ettin-reranker-v1-data#lighton-pre-training-32-configs, I limited the largest sources from embeddings-pre-training to 5M and smaller ones to 2.5M, but during my tests I also tried limiting the largest to 1M and the smallest to 500k. Expanding to the larger number of rows was beneficial. I might also benefit from going larger, but that was exceeding my training time goals. I only experimented with the number of embeddings-fine-tuning data by updating its sampling (e.g. the top 64 has 2x as much fine-tuning data as the top 32 test).

I ended up not wanting to do too many experiments on the data mixture, as I was wary that I might start to overfit on my evaluation benchmark (NanoBEIR), which would only result in better NanoBEIR scores but worse overall MTEB scores. So I didn't do too much.

In ST, you advise to discard Arguana and Touché when using Nanobeir13, I guess it works best with those at the end ?

In truth, I probably should not have excluded these 2 from the default CrossEncoderNanoBEIREvaluator, as people might run the dense and reranker evaluators side by side and expect to be able to compare them, which you now sadly can't do. But in short: At the time, my opinion was that Arguana and Touche2020 didn't really match the usual usage for rerankers. For example, in ArguAna the query is just a big paragraph, and in Touche the documents are a bit vague (i.e. not as confident information sources but instead opinions). I think these might make them less suited as benchmarking datasets for reranker models, and I suppose also less interesting as training datasets for training rerankers. In the blogpost, I included them, as I want the scores to be easier to compare to the dense NanoBEIR13 scores from a standard embedding model.

The discussion about keeping rerankers usable and avoiding overfitting to NanoBEIR is valuable. For deployment comparisons I'd also like to see quality and p50/p95 end-to-end latency at a fixed candidate count, plus a lexical-recall ceiling. We recently evaluated batched semantic judgments on a narrow BM25 candidate pool and reported server and client timings separately: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't tested Ettin on that set, so this is not a model comparison. Are there published CPU latency measurements for the smaller Ettin variants at a fixed batch size?
